articles.title: The internet's favorite dancing 'Rumpelstiltskin' meme has a surprising origin
articles.summary: That viral "Rumpelstiltskin" meme you're seeing everywhere? It's AI. But its faux Hollywood backstory "may invite more curiosity and sharing," says an expert...
articles.body:
As the kids like to say: "That's so AI."

We're talking about the viral Rumpelstiltskin meme you may have seen — or even shared — on social media. The unusual-looking character has been dancing across feeds, often set to rapper Riff Raff's song "Tip Toe Wing in My Jawwdinz."

One TikTok user described the scene as the "type of dreams I be having after taking dollar store melatonin."

In other versions, he's raiding the fridge at 2 a.m. and dancing in Payless shoes.

Alongside the jokes, there's been confusion about where this odd scene originated. Some thought the tuxedoed toe-tapper was real footage from the 1987 movie Rumpelstiltskin — a musical fairy tale starring Amy Irving as the miller's daughter and Billy Barty as the scheming straw-to-gold spinner.

The viral character isn't Barty, though. As NBC reports, the clip is AI-generated , even if people may think they remember watching it long ago in the fantasy flick.

What's interesting is that it being AI doesn't necessarily spoil the fun. Raju Narisetti , who leads global publishing and marketing at McKinsey & Company and follows the intersection of AI, creativity and audience behavior, suspects that people sharing a funny meme aren't especially concerned with how it was made.

"If it makes them laugh, surprises them or gives them something amusing to pass along, that's often seemingly enough," he tells Yahoo.

Besides, research suggests AI-generated humor can land with audiences too. A 2025 study by researchers in Sweden and Germany found that, on average, AI-generated memes scored higher on humor, creativity and shareability than those made by people or human-AI teams. Humans still had the edge in humor among the top-performing memes, however.

Where in the crazy internet realm did the Rumpelstiltskin meme come from?

Know Your Meme traces the footage to an Aug. 27 Instagram post shared by @Stroinaya with accounts @Neuroferma and @anna_glinskaya_creatorai listed as collaborators.

The caption, in Russian, promotes a course on making AI films without actors, a camera or a big budget. The sequence resembles an old movie: A Rumpelstiltskin-like character walks into a straw-filled room where a woman is crying. She looks terrified at first, but then he starts dancing — and the straw turns into gold coins. Money changes everything, and suddenly she's so happy she kisses him and he transforms into a prince.

The original meme now has 1.7 million views — and its own Instagram .

In September, it started to snowball with the pumping addition of Riff Raff's 2014 ode to his sneakers and playful captions. That's what led to it being dubbed the "Rumpelstiltskin tiptoeing in my Jordans" meme — and it's become meme generator gold . Not to mention last-minute Halloween costume inspiration.

Along the way, some mistook its throwback look for having an actual cinematic connection. Then came the explainers about its AI, not Hollywood, origins.

Why does it feel like you've seen it before?

For some viewers, the confusion went beyond guessing which movie the clip came from. They felt they'd seen it before.

"There's some Mandela effect shit going on then, because I swear I've been seeing this guy for years," wrote an Instagram commenter.

The "Mandela effect " refers to a shared false memory. It takes its name from people incorrectly remembering that Nelson Mandela died in prison in the 1980s. He actually died in 2013, after being released in 1990 and going on to serve as South Africa's president.

University of Chicago researchers studied the visual form of the Mandela effect, including the widespread tendency to remember the Monopoly Man wearing a monocle. (He doesn't.) The research found that people can confidently make the same mistakes when recalling familiar characters.

Those findings don't confirm what's happening with this particular meme. But the comments show how convincing its apparent cinematic past has been.

Advances in AI are making it even more challenging to spot fakes . As we've seen with fake Met Gala arrivals in recent years and impostor Ryan Goslings , differentiating between real life and digital creation isn't always easy.

But figuring out how a meme was made and understanding why people like it are different questions. Narisetti suspects that, in this case, the supposed Hollywood backstory adds to its appeal.

"A clip that appears to be an obscure piece of 1980s movie history may invite more curiosity and sharing than one presented upfront as AI-generated," says Narisetti. "That backstory gives people something to discover, discuss and perhaps feel clever about recognizing."

But for Narisetti, honesty around a clip's origin matters.

"There's nothing inherently wrong with enjoying or sharing AI-generated entertainment, I think, but when a fictional origin is presented as fact, it raises a different issue about authenticity and trust," he says.

"We can enjoy the joke while still caring whether the story attached to it is true."

articles.title: Dame Judi Dench joins call to keep Archers in Birmingham
articles.summary: The cast have described plans to leave Birmingham as similar "to Corrie leaving the north-west."
articles.body:
More than 100 current and former cast and crew members of The Archers, including Dame Judi Dench, have called on the BBC to keep the programme in Birmingham.

The appeal follows a decision to shelve plans for a dedicated studio at the broadcaster's new Digbeth headquarters.

Supporters say recording the drama elsewhere could affect its quality and future.

The BBC says the move is part of wider cost-saving measures and alternative options are being explored.

In a letter to director general Matt Brittin, actors, writers, directors and sound engineers argued that moving recordings away from the Midlands would have a "tangible impact" on the programme.

The letter compares the prospect to "Coronation Street leaving the north-west, or EastEnders leaving the south-east", adding that it risks "ripping out the heart of Ambridge".

Signatories said Birmingham had been central to the show's identity since it began and warned that separating cast and production teams could affect the way the programme is made.

"A flagship show deserves flagship facilities, from which both the BBC and the city of Birmingham would benefit for decades," the letter said.

It was signed by more than 100 current and former cast and crew members, including Dench, Felicity Jones and Kellie Bright, as well as representatives from Equity and the Writers' Guild.

The Archers, set in the fictional West Midlands village of Ambridge, celebrated its 75th anniversary earlier this year and has always been recorded in Birmingham.

The intervention follows the BBC's announcement that plans for a bespoke studio at its new Tea Factory headquarters in Digbeth would not go ahead.

The Worcestershire village of Inkberrow is believed to have inspired the show's fictional village of Ambridge, while The Old Bull Inn is closely associated with the show's pub, The Bull.

Speaking earlier this week, Brittin defended the decision , saying the BBC needed to make savings but remained committed to the programme.

"We're going to explore how we can best house The Archers where they need to be," he said.

He added there was "other studio space around the country" which could accommodate the programme, while alternatives in the West Midlands would also be considered.

West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker also called for the show to remain in Birmingham, describing it as a key part of the region's broadcasting heritage.

Equity general secretary Paul Fleming said cast members were "angry" at the proposals.

"It's beyond offensive, I think, for any Midlander, the idea that you would record something that is so iconic and so ironically about the Midlands, anywhere other than in the region where it's set," he told BBC Radio 4.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Mystery drones over UK' and 'Troops heading to Poland for war games'
articles.summary: The Daily Telegraph leads with reports that RAF jets had two close encounters with unidentified drones earlier this year.
articles.body:
The Times reports that hundreds of British troops will head to Poland next month to rehearse deploying to Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire . The paper says personnel from Germany and France will also be involved - and the exercise will simulate moving troops and logistical supplies, such as food and fuel.

The Daily Telegraph says RAF jets reported close encounters with two unidentified drones in British skies earlier this year . What the paper calls the "near misses" happened just days apart during simulated air combat training and an air-to-air refuelling exercise over the North Sea.

According to the Guardian, Devon and Cornwall Police has apologised and paid compensation to nine women after the force was accused of promoting and protecting male officers despite knowing they were suspected of domestic abuse. The force denies claims that it covered up the crimes but has vowed to improve how it protects women.

"Will Musk's flying car take off" , asks the Times - one of several papers to feature photos from the launch of the Tesla Roadster 2. The FT Weekend says "the sports car flies vertically up in the air, hovers and even flies upside down" - and describes the demonstration as "scenes more familiar to a Back to the Future film". The Daily Star picks up that theme - comparing the Tesla to the time-travelling DeLorean from the film - concluding: "Let's hope it doesn't need 1.21 gigawatts of plutonium to run".

images.caption: The Daily Telegraph leads with reports that RAF jets had two close encounters with unidentified drones earlier this year while they were completing training exercises over the North Sea. The paper says the "near-misses" took place just days apart, and the mystery objects were spotted at 17,000ft - which it notes is more than 40 times the legal height limit for commercial drones. Incident logs, which have been seen by the newspaper, suggest that the RAF reported the sightings to police and "multiple different external investigations" are ongoing.

articles.title: Depressão sorridente: como identificar sinais da condição atípica | G1
articles.standfirst: Quem parece feliz por fora, mas sofre por dentro, pode ter uma forma atípica de depressão. Mas esconder o que realmente sente pode prejudicar a saúde mental
articles.summary: A depressão sorridente é uma forma atípica da doença em que o sofrimento é mascarado, o que pode agravar a saúde mental e dificultar a busca por ajuda médica.
articles.body:
A 'depressão sorridente' não é um diagnóstico oficialmente reconhecido, mas as buscas pela expressão cresceram 50% nos últimos cinco anos — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Quando imaginamos alguém com depressão, é comum imaginar uma pessoa que mal consegue sair da cama.

Alguém que chora com frequência, se afasta dos amigos ou não tem energia para enfrentar o dia.

Dificilmente pensamos em uma pessoa que faz piadas durante o jantar, mantém uma vida social agitada e se destaca no trabalho.

Mas essa pode ser justamente a realidade de quem vive com a chamada "depressão sorridente".

E, às vezes, a pessoa que não percebe o que está acontecendo é você mesmo.

Segundo a OMS, cerca de 322 milhões de pessoas no mundo têm depressão — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

A "depressão sorridente" não é um diagnóstico oficialmente reconhecido, mas as buscas pelo termo aumentaram 50% nos últimos cinco anos.

"[O termo] significa parecer feliz por fora, enquanto, por dentro, você se sente deprimido e desanimado", diz Olivia Remes, pesquisadora de saúde mental da Universidade de Cambridge, no Reino Unido.

Todos nós nos sentimos desanimados de vez em quando. Mas, segundo a Organização Mundial da Saúde ( OMS ), 322 milhões de pessoas no mundo sofrem de depressão.

A condição se caracteriza por sintomas como tristeza persistente ou perda de interesse e prazer, que se prolongam por semanas ou meses e afetam o trabalho, os relacionamentos, o sono e a rotina.

Mas a depressão nem sempre se manifesta da maneira que imaginamos. Estudos sugerem que até 40% das pessoas com a condição apresentam uma forma "atípica", com sintomas que fogem dos padrões mais conhecidos.

Em vez de perder o apetite ou dormir menos, por exemplo, a pessoa pode passar a comer ou dormir mais do que o habitual.

Seu humor também pode melhorar temporariamente diante de uma experiência positiva ou empolgante.

Há ainda evidências de que pessoas com depressão podem esconder o que estão passando por meio da chamada camuflagem, também conhecida como mascaramento.

Que é uma tentativa de ocultar determinadas características ou emoções para se adaptar ao convívio social.

Por que as pessoas escondem a depressão?

Algumas pessoas com "depressão sorridente" nem sequer percebem que estão deprimidas e, por isso, não sabem que estão escondendo a condição.

"Elas podem achar que seus sintomas são apenas consequência de uma vida agitada e estressante", diz Remes, da Universidade de Cambridge.

Outras reconhecem que estão passando por dificuldades, mas fazem de tudo para que ninguém perceba. Esse comportamento é particularmente comum entre pessoas perfeccionistas e com um forte senso de responsabilidade.

"Elas têm expectativas elevadas em relação a si mesmas e podem não querer admitir, nem para si nem para os outros, que estão enfrentando dificuldades", afirma Remes.

Algumas pessoas temem o estigma e receiam sobrecarregar os outros. Estudos mostram que outras pessoas podem se preocupar com o julgamento alheio ou com possíveis consequências no trabalho ou nos relacionamentos.

As expectativas da família e as normas culturais também podem dificultar uma conversa aberta sobre o assunto.

Quais são os riscos de esconder a depressão?

Especialistas alertam que o esforço para manter as aparências pode trazer riscos.

"A depressão nos isola e nos faz sentir sozinhos. Muitas vezes, um dos melhores antídotos para o desânimo é se conectar com outras pessoas", diz Barney Dunn, professor e psicólogo clínico da Universidade de Exeter, também no Reino Unido.

Ao esconder a depressão, a pessoa também pode deixar de receber a ajuda de que precisa.

"Esses sinais iniciais, se não forem tratados, podem se agravar e evoluir para um quadro crônico e grave, além de aumentar o risco de suicídio", afirma Remes, da Universidade de Cambridge.

Sete sinais de depressão que podem passar despercebidos

Uma sensibilidade maior do que o habitual a críticas ou à rejeição pode ser um sinal de depressão — Foto: Getty Images

Mesmo quem parece estar lidando bem com a vida pode apresentar mudanças de comportamento que merecem atenção.

1. Você deixa de sentir prazer nas coisas

Encontrar os amigos, ir à academia ou assistir ao seu programa de TV favorito eram atividades que você aguardava com entusiasmo, mas agora parecem uma obrigação? Essa mudança pode ser um sinal de que algo não vai bem.

"É fácil atribuir a falta de prazer ou de interesse nos passatempos habituais à correria e ao ritmo acelerado da vida", diz Remes.

2. Você sente um peso incomum nos braços ou nas pernas

Uma sensação de peso nos braços e nas pernas, que torna os movimentos do dia a dia mais difíceis, pode ser um sinal de depressão atípica.

Esse sintoma é conhecido como "paralisia de chumbo".

3. Você cancela compromissos com frequência

Às vezes, você pode parecer na sua "melhor forma" quando está com outras pessoas, mas acabar cancelando compromissos nos dias em que seu humor piora e fica mais difícil esconder o que está sentindo.

4. Você dorme mais, mas continua sentindo exaustão

Mesmo com um cansaço cada vez maior, você pode continuar cumprindo todas as suas atividades habituais.

"As noites podem ser particularmente difíceis", diz Remes, "pois as pessoas com essa condição podem se sentir pior no fim do dia e precisar de mais sono do que o habitual".

5. Você fica mais sensível a críticas ou à rejeição

Um comentário casual do chefe ou um compromisso cancelado por um amigo pode magoar muito mais do que antes.

Segundo Remes, essa sensibilidade maior a críticas ou à rejeição é uma característica da depressão atípica. O mesmo sintoma também pode ocorrer em pessoas com transtorno de déficit de atenção e hiperatividade (TDAH).

6. Você é sempre a pessoa engraçada ou prestativa

Uma pessoa com depressão nem sempre se afasta dos outros. Muitas vezes, pode fazer o oposto: ser quem anima a festa, se dedicar intensamente ao trabalho ou se desdobrar para ajudar outras pessoas.

7. Seus pensamentos sobre si são sempre negativos

Você pode transmitir confiança aos outros, mas ser extremamente crítico consigo mesmo.

Duvidar constantemente de si, sentir que não tem valor ou ter pensamentos marcados por uma sensação de vazio são possíveis sinais de alerta.

O próprio termo "depressão sorridente" recebe críticas.

Remes, da Universidade de Cambridge, afirma que embora possa ajudar as pessoas a identificar e dar nome ao que estão vivendo, a expressão também corre o risco de "simplificar demais" uma experiência complexa.

"A palavra 'sorridente' faz pensar em alegria e felicidade", diz a pesquisadora, mas "a característica central dessa condição é, na verdade, a falta de esperança, o vazio e a sensação de não ter valor".

Para Dunn, da Universidade de Exeter, um primeiro passo pode ser compartilhar, aos poucos, o que você está sentindo com alguém de confiança.

"Muitas vezes, as pessoas se surpreendem ao perceber que isso pode fortalecer os vínculos com os outros, ajudá-las a se sentir conectadas e a entender que não são as únicas a se sentir assim", diz o professor.

O especialista também recomenda procurar um médico caso você esteja enfrentando dificuldades.

"Há boas evidências de que conversar, usar medicamentos [antidepressivos] e receber intervenções sociais podem ser medidas eficazes", afirma Dunn.

Caso você seja ou conheça alguém que apresente sinais de alerta relacionados ao suicídio, ou tenha perdido uma pessoa querida para o suicídio, confira alguns locais para pedir ajuda:

O Centro de Valorização da Vida (CVV), por meio do telefone 188, oferece atendimento gratuito 24h por dia; há também a opção de conversa por chat, e-mail e busca por postos de atendimento em todo o Brasil;

Para jovens de 13 a 24 anos, a Unicef oferece também o chat Pode Falar;

Em casos de emergência, outra recomendação de especialistas é ligar para os Bombeiros ( telefone 193 ) ou para a Polícia Militar ( telefone 190 );

Outra opção é ligar para o SAMU, pelo telefone 192 ;

Na rede pública local, é possível buscar ajuda também nos Centros de Atenção Psicossocial (CAPS), em Unidades Básicas de Saúde (UBS) e Unidades de Pronto Atendimento (UPA) 24h;

Confira também o Mapa da Saúde Mental , que ajuda a encontrar atendimento em saúde mental gratuito em todo o Brasil.

Para aqueles que perderam alguém para o suicídio, a Associação Brasileira dos Sobreviventes Enlutados por Suicídio (Abrases) oferece assistência e grupos de apoio.

articles.title: Filho transforma pai agricultor em drag queen para sessão de fotos no PR: 'Quero, por um dia, poder te mostrar como eu pertenço no mundo' | G1
articles.standfirst: Na exposição, o fotógrafo Danilo Zocatteli registrou o pai, João Zocatelli, maquiado e com uma peruca em atividades do dia a dia na roça. Pai e filho relatam que projeto mudou a relação entre eles.
articles.summary: Na exposição do fotógrafo Danilo Zocatteli, o pai, João Zocatelli, aparece enquadrado em atividades do dia a dia na roça. Pai e filho relatam que projeto mudou a relação entre eles
articles.body:
Quatro horas de maquiagem transformaram João Zocatelli, de 64 anos, de agricultor em drag queen . Com peruca, brilho e diversas cores no rosto, ele posou para uma sessão de fotos caracterizado como uma personagem drag em um cenário rural de Marialva , no Norte do Paraná.

Nas imagens, João aparece maquiado, com suas roupas de agricultor, em atividades cotidianas da roça, como o abate de animais e o transporte pelas plantações. As fotos foram feitas pelo filho de João, o fotógrafo Danilo Zocatteli, de 37 anos. O projeto é parte de uma pesquisa de mestrado dele na universidade Royal College of Art, de Londres, no Reino Unido.

Para Danilo, os registros representam mais do que o apoio de pai para filho, mas também uma "troca de papéis". Ao g1 , o fotógrafo explicou que, por morar no exterior, quando visitava os pais no Brasil, sentia que tinha uma personalidade diferente da que tem no país europeu – era como se ele montasse um personagem ao chegar na cidade em que cresceu.

João Zocatelli na fotografia intitulada 'Querido pai, parece que ir embora foi necessário para que eu entendesse que precisava voltar'. — Foto: Danilo Zocatelli

"Eu sempre tinha essa necessidade de estar, de certa forma, performando uma certa masculinidade devido ao ambiente em que cresci. E eu via que, todas as vezes que eu voltava para o Brasil, eu ia me desmontando. Eu tinha uma vida lá [na Inglaterra], uma forma de me expressar e tinha uma curiosidade, e aí, quando eu vinha para o Brasil, eu tinha uma outra", relatou.

O convite para que o pai posasse para as fotos foi também um convite para que os dois pudessem se compreender melhor. A partir desse sentimento e com a vontade de criar um projeto "chocante", como Danilo mesmo define, a iniciativa tomou forma.

Registros do pai ao longo dos anos integram uma das peças do trabalho de Danilo Zocatelli. — Foto: Danilo Zocatelli/Acervo Pessoal

O convite demorou cerca de cinco segundos para ser aceito, lembra Danilo. "Ele me disse: 'Só vou fazer se você comprar uma peruca bonita para mim e para sua mãe. Mas tem que ser com uma peruca bonita'", conta.

Ao introduzir a ideia, Danilo explicou que as fotos só fariam sentido com a participação do pai e adiantou que o processo poderia fazer surgir assuntos sobre os quais nunca haviam conversado antes.

Entre a maquiagem e a poeira da roça, as sessões de fotos acabaram indo além do experimento artístico, provocando uma transformação na maneira como pai e filho se enxergam. O intuito, segundo Danilo, nunca foi mudar o jeito do agricultor, mas sim que ele possa sentir como o fotógrafo se sente, pelo menos uma vez.

"Eu só quero, por um dia, poder te mostrar como eu pertenço no mundo, como eu me sinto. Eu quero te olhar e me ver refletido em você, sem ter medo de ser assim como sou — gay, cabelo comprido, brincos, piercing e unhas pintadas", diz Danilo em uma carta ao pai.

'Querido pai, acredito que encontramos nossa paz' — Foto: Danilo Zocatelli

João conta que se sentiu um pouco apreensivo quando se olhou no espelho pela primeira vez após ser maquiado. O choque inicial foi dando espaço ao sentimento de carinho por poder fazer parte de algo tão importante para o filho. "Tudo que foi da minha parte, eu fiz. Sem reclamar, tudo de boa", diz.

Uma das primeiras reações do agricultor foi enviar uma foto para um amigo. "O amigo é alemão. Ele só disse que, se eu precisasse de uma drag loira, era só chamar", contou Danilo.

João passou um dia tentando sentir como o filho se sente no mundo. Danilo também aproveitou a experiência para reconhecer beleza nos detalhes da rotina rural do pai.

"O meu pai é uma pessoa muito, muito sábia. Ele tem uma capacidade de pegar milhões de sementes, colocá-las no solo, fazer com que elas cresçam, floresçam, nasçam, mas tem muitas coisas que são limitações para ele, assim como para mim. Eu não sei fazer o que ele faz. Então, ver esse homem do campo, vestido de drag, em cima de um trator, com a barriguinha aparecendo, segurando um pano pink voando, é uma imagem que eu nunca imaginaria ver", diz Danilo.

'Querido Pai, Te olhar na sua roupa de sítio com a cara pintada e usando uma peruca enorme foi como todo filho deveria ver seu pai um heroi'. — Foto: Danilo Zocatelli

'Todo mundo que me encontra fala alguma coisa'

Foram cinco dias de maquiagens, fotografias e caminhadas pela zona rural da cidade. A paisagem de Marialva, familiar para os dois, ganhou novos contornos à medida que Danilo eternizava a figura do pai e encontrava velhos conhecidos pelo caminho.

O clima ao redor das filmagens era de curiosidade. Quem encontrava João e Danilo no campo de futebol, na lavoura, no celeiro, na igreja ou em meio ao abate de um carneiro, parava para ver o que estava acontecendo. Apesar da surpresa, o mais comum era que a abordagem terminasse em risadas e elogios.

"Todo mundo que me encontra fala alguma coisa. A cada pouco vem um elogio, um abraço de uma pessoa. E isso aí foi muito forte para mim. Eu ter aceitado e ter essa repercussão", relata João.

As fotografias do projeto 'Querido Pai' passaram por exposições artísticas na Inglaterra, França e Bélgica. A partir de 5 de dezembro, ficam à mostra na Justiça Federal do Rio de Janeiro.

articles.title: Mais de 90 mil óculos irregulares foram apreendidos em Porto Alegre | G1
articles.standfirst: Produtos vendidos sem avaliação individual podem causar distorções na imagem e fazer com que doenças oculares fiquem sem diagnóstico.
articles.summary: Mais de 90 mil óculos falsificados foram apreendidos em Porto Alegre. Produtos sem medidas individuais podem causar desconforto e atrasar diagnósticos.
articles.body:
Mais de 90 mil óculos falsificados foram apreendidos em Porto Alegre nos últimos 18 meses , segundo a prefeitura. Vendidos sem receita, medidas individualizadas ou garantia de procedência, esses produtos podem causar desconforto e atrasar o diagnóstico de doenças oculares.

O comércio irregular ocorre principalmente na região central da capital . Nas calçadas, clientes experimentam diferentes modelos até encontrar um que pareça melhorar a visão. Em um dos flagrantes, um vendedor raspa uma lente no chão para tentar encaixá-la em uma armação .

Segundo a prefeitura, os óculos apreendidos são destruídos e recebem a destinação considerada adequada pelo município. A legislação prevê multa e apreensão imediata. A fiscalização passa diariamente pela região central, mas moradores também podem denunciar a venda irregular pelo telefone 156.

A facilidade de compra, a quantidade de produtos disponíveis e os preços baixos ajudam a atrair clientes . No entanto, a escolha feita apenas pela aparente melhora da visão não considera a causa da dificuldade para enxergar .

O diretor-executivo do Sindióptica-RS, Roberto Tenedini, afirma que nem todo problema de visão está relacionado à necessidade de usar óculos. Segundo ele, a compra sem avaliação pode criar uma falsa sensação de que o problema foi resolvido.

"Na verdade, é uma grande ilusão, porque nem sempre a questão da visão está relacionada à questão do uso do óculos. Muitas vezes está relacionada às questões patológicas, que vão de diabetes, pressão alta, né? E a pessoa deixa, na verdade, de verificar uma possibilidade de ter na sua saúde uma reparação com relação às questões patológicas para poder compensar com esse tipo de produto, achando que realmente está bem assistido", disse.

De acordo com o Fórum Nacional Contra a Pirataria e a ilegalidade, o setor de óculos é o quinto mais afetado pela pirataria e pela ilegalidade no Brasil .

O presidente da Sociedade de Oftalmologia do Rio Grande do Sul, Guilherme Diehl, explica que a adaptação das lentes depende de medidas individuais. Entre elas estão a centração da lente, a posição do centro óptico e a distância naso-pupilar .

"A gente não sabe a qualidade óptica da lente, as medidas de centração dessa lente, do centro óptico ou a medida de cada paciente, que é a distância naso-pupilar. Isso tudo pode causar distorções na imagem, visão mais cansada, astenopia e uma má qualidade óptica", afirmou.

Segundo Diehl, o principal risco é de que a melhora inicial faça a pessoa adiar uma consulta oftalmológica. Com isso, doenças potencialmente graves para a visão podem ficar sem diagnóstico .

"A pessoa usando esse óculos, ela se sente atendida e deixa de procurar o atendimento oftalmológico tradicional, completo, onde vai ser analisada visão, medida de pressão do olho, exame de fundo de olho. O uso desse óculos afasta o paciente, a pessoa do consultório oftalmológico e pode deixar para trás algumas doenças que podem ser potencialmente graves para a visão", disse.

articles.title: US coastguard rescues 16 after boat sinks off Mexico’s Baja coast
articles.summary: Eleven people are believed to be still missing, with rescue operations under way.
articles.body:
The US coastguard has said it rescued 16 people from the Pacific Ocean after a boat sank off Mexico’s Baja California coast.

The coastguard said on Friday it responded to a Mayday call reporting that a boat was sinking. The search is ongoing for 11 people believed to be still missing.

The boat went down about 225km (140 miles) west of Ensenada, Mexico.

A rescue helicopter reached the site about two hours after someone on the boat transmitted the Mayday call at about 1am (08:00 GMT) on Friday, said coastguard Lieutenant Santiago Tamburini.

It took about 90 minutes for the coastguard crew, which included a rescue swimmer, to pull the 16 people from the water, Tamburini said.

The people rescued were Mexican nationals, according to the Mexican consulate.

One survivor was being treated for a suspected shark bite and two were in critical condition, authorities said.

The rescued were flown by helicopter to San Diego, California, and transported to hospitals. The Mexican consulate in San Diego said it offered consular assistance.

The coastguard and US Navy are continuing to search the area with two helicopters, a fixed-wing plane, a cutter and a navy combat ship.

The boat sank in an area frequented by smugglers transporting migrants to the US. It is also popular with fishing and leisure boats.

Details about the boat’s origin, destination and what it was doing are not clear. No vessel, only debris, was found, and it was unclear what type of boat was involved, the coastguard said.

“Boats in that area can be for fishing, leisure, personal recreation. We just don’t know what they were doing out there. We all know it’s a suspected smuggling route,” Tamburini said.

articles.title: Miranda's tears, joy and dance moves steal show as celebrities battle deadly boredom on The Traitors
articles.summary: Miranda Hart became emotional and spoke about her health problems as more action unfolded on Friday.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode six of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

For a show that likes to keep participants and viewers on the edges of their seats, gripped by suspense and skullduggery, it was ironic that Friday's episode of The Celebrity Traitors came down to which one of its stars would die of boredom.

The climactic final scene switched between a series of faces as we waited to see which of the famous faithful would... yawn.

Some dramatic editing and music attempted to build fevered anticipation, but this was a slow-motion, low-energy premise for a murder in plain sight.

The trio of traitors had been tasked with being as boring as possible, and yawned theatrically in one of the castle's communal rooms in the hope that their apparent fatigue would be contagious.

If one of the faithful succumbs to the traitors' soporific tactics and yawns as well, they will be put to sleep for good.

We must wait until next Thursday to find out who, if anyone, is murdered in plain sight. That was what passed as a nail-biting cliffhanger this week.

There was, thankfully, some more animated action elsewhere in Friday's episode.

After Thursday saw King Kenny recruited by the traitors - that episode ending with his deliciously evil laugh - the YouTuber and former aspiring boxer brought fresh and fiendish energy to the turret.

"This threesome's going to be different," mama traitor Maya Jama predicted. "There's a new vibrance."

James Acaster, her reluctant fellow traitor, was also happy with their choice of ally.

"As predicted, Kenny's taken to this like a duck to water," the comedian said, visibly relieved. "He's the opposite of me. So relaxed. He's a natural born traitor."

Kenny is relishing the role, barely able to disguise his pleasure as Miranda Hart confided to him over breakfast that "you're my main faithful".

The self-declared modern-day Miss Marple warned Kenny to be on the lookout for anyone acting differently, reasoning that "if you're suddenly a traitor, you're going to be a bit on high alert".

"I agree," was his straight-faced reply.

In the show's diary room, he said: "The first taste of being on the other side - it does feel good, because you have the power.

"I'm good at staying calm because as a boxer you have to have a poker face. You can't let the other people know that you're intimidated."

However, he later admitted: "On the outside I look calm, cool, collected, but on the inside I'm incredibly nervous."

Meanwhile, all eyes were on a different player as the traitors' possible new recruit.

The previous day, Joe Lycett had loudly declared that he longed for a ticket to the turret - and even though it would have been, as he later protested, too obvious for the traitors to grant him his wish, it was enough to arouse suspicion.

Acaster observed: "I feel like today is one of those days where maybe we [traitors] don't even have to do anything. You have no idea of the gift that I've been given."

And in a game where the group often latches on to any conspicuous sign of questionable behaviour, Acaster's prediction was confirmed.

"I sort of laid my own trap, and now I'm in it," Lycett conceded ruefully before he headed to the round table. He received 11 of the 14 votes.

Standing in front of his fellow celebrities before being whisked out of the castle, he informed them: "I always wanted to start as a faithful and end as a traitor.

"I started as a faithful. I did not get my wish. I am a faithful."

One of the few who did not vote for Joe was Miranda. In fact, she was laughed at around the table for not being able to bring herself to write her friend's name.

So when his faithful status was revealed, she exclaimed: "Oh my God, my love was real!"

The pair had formed a bond, and her tearful reaction to his exit provided a rare poignant moment.

"Connection and laughter and joy are bigger than this game - and to meet someone and just play and laugh, it's all us humans need, you know?" she said.

"I've had times in my life when I haven't had that, through illness, and it's brought up that silly, sensitive soul."

The comedian revealed two years ago that she had been bed-bound and housebound with chronic fatigue after being diagnosed with Lyme disease.

“Suddenly the floodgates were kind of opening. It was suddenly not about a silly faithful or traitor, you know?”

Miranda also referenced that difficult period during Friday's mission, when the players had to collect and assemble parts of Easter Island-like statues on a rainy hillside.

"Three or four years ago, due to illness, I thought that I may not ever have a gentle walk around a park again," she said.

"And I find myself up a Scottish Highland, wheelbarrowing along a very large head. It's really exciting."

Miranda has been one of the most astute faithfuls (despite not sniffing out Kenny's switched allegiances, yet), but has also proved to be one of the most likeable celebrities.

And she provided the clear highlight of the show on Friday - not during a mission or a round table or a scheming chat, but when pop star Leigh-Anne Pinnock offered to console her by making her "dreams come true" and teaching her a Little Mix dance move.

"Introducing Little Mix and... Big Mix!" Miranda said as the pair wiggled and thrusted gleefully on the floor.

Someone should give her her own TV show.

Miranda and Leigh-Anne were blissfully unaware that next door, something much more boring but ultimately more consequential was unfolding.

The traitors had been tasked with spraying "deadly sleeping powder" from a perfume bottle and then murdering one of the faithful in plain sight by making them inhale it by yawning.

They had little choice about their potential victims - in the end it was Jerry Hall and Ross Kemp who wandered in to join Maya and James A in deliberately tedious conversation.

It was a set-up so convoluted that it's doubtful that even Ross, who has been permanently paranoid about being murdered in plain sight, rumbled them.

Maya and James A were left yawning ever more widely in the desperate hope that the other two would join in, before the credits rolled. The most grippingly boring TV of the year.

articles.title: Actress Selma Blair says she 'did not intend to harm anyone' in plane altercation
articles.summary: A publicist for the actress said the incident stemmed from a "medical emergency" and said she has a neurological disorder that can cause out-of-control responses.
articles.body:
US actress Selma Blair has spoken out after being accused of assaulting multiple people on a flight travelling to New York.

A publicist for the Legally Blonde star said she "did not intend to harm anyone" and there was "much more to this story". Blair "experienced a medical emergency on the flight" and is still fighting ​multiple sclerosis (MS), the statement read.

The statement says that Blair, 54, has a neurological disorder that "bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her".

The star pleaded not guilty to charges that she assaulted an officer and a nurse after being removed from the flight. She was also accused of assulting two flight attendants on board.

In a statement to the BBC, Blair's team said the public account of what happened to her aboard a Delta Airlines flight to New York "has been built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline". They also denied media reports that she had attempted to open the door of the aircraft.

The publicist noted Blair's fight against multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic illness the actress revealed publicly in 2018. She announced in 2021 that she was in remission for the disease, but the statement notes that the Hellboy and Cruel Intentions star "still has bad days".

It adds that she also has pseudobulbar affect (PBA) - a disorder that develops in the context of a brain injury or underlying neurological dysfunction, according to the US National Institutes of Health.

The disorder affects emotional expression that can result in sudden involuntary, and out-of-control episodes of laughing, crying, or anger that do not match how a person actually feels.

She described Blair's physical achievements since her MS diagnosis as "nothing short of a miracle" and noted that she still lives with pain daily.

"Selma had never been arrested before Sunday night," the statement said. "There is much more to this story than has been reported, and we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgment, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion."

The incident happened on a flight travelling from Los Angeles to New York on Sunday evening. New York airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on a Delta Airlines flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.

A pilot asked for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to audio recorded on air traffic control obtained by CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

Blair was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons by the FBI for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US that relates to the on-board altercation.

The two additional charges of assault were filed in state court after she was taken off the plane. She has pleaded not guilty to those charges and was released on bail.

With additional reporting by Rebecka Pieder.

articles.title: Faisal Islam: What I learned from a week with the world's top finance leaders
articles.summary: At the IMF meeting in Bangkok this week finance and business leaders grappled with uncertainty.
articles.body:
When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.

There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies.

Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity.

At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go.

In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France.

However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions.

In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US.

Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing.

And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis.

Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget

'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK

Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF

But there is a third big challenge to wrestle with, on top of geopolitical instability and bond market uncertainty, one that's apparent even on the streets of Bangkok, as the chauffeurs dropped off the bankers and finance ministers for this week's gathering.

Like other nations Thailand has experienced first hand the astonishing boom in sales of Chinese electric vehicles. Thailand is sometimes dubbed the "Detroit of Asia" for its own strong car making heritage. Now nearly a third of all car sales are Chinese EVs.

It is the clearest example of what is known as the China Shock Two. The sheer speed of China's dominance in advanced manufacturing. The first China shock came in the 2000s in basic manufacturing.

This second wave of dramatic change has led in just the last few months to a reappraisal of how world trade is functioning and how it is going to be managed. This is especially the case in the EU, which is scrambling to reassess what currently feels like a one-way street when it comes to China-Europe trade.

The extra "Made in Europe" protections that the bloc is drawing up will have a profound impact on the UK too. If the UK is outside the new rules, China could divert its excess car production to the UK, where, like Thailand, there are currently lower tariffs and even subsidies. Or the EU could invite Britain in, but ask it to follow its suit by raising tariffs to match its own.

Then there is the sub-plot of the UK's relationship with the European Union. This was a theme that cut through more than might have been expected in Bangkok this week and even seemed to provide a little entertainment. The managing director of the IMF Kristalina Georgieva rolled with laughter, suggesting the Brexit "divorcees are now dating again". The Finnish finance minister told me the UK was "flirting" with the EU. Major banks were issuing reports about the prospect of "Breturn".

It is, however, the AI boom that is being relied on to provide the trampoline that is required to bounce the world economy out of its current era of multiple simultaneous crises, so many of which are linked to the decisions of President Trump.

But even that is not clear cut. In one room the transformative economic effect of AI is lionised by finance ministers. In the next, central bankers fret about its power to break the cybersecurity of most of the banking system. The financial boom around it can't last. The masters of the financial universe are just thankful that it has so far.

articles.title: Trump waives Russia-related sanctions before they even kick in as Ukraine ties worsen
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has waived a further slate of sanctions related to Russian fossil fuel sales, days before they were to take effect under a bill he signed into law last month.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has waived a further slate of sanctions related to Russian fossil fuel sales, days before they were to take effect under a bill he signed into law last month. The waiver announced in an executive order Friday comes as Trump increasingly feuds with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and cracks appear in Washington’s support for Kyiv in its four-year-old war against its invading neighbor, deepening alarm among European allies. The White House has heaped pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities, as it seeks to ease oil prices ahead of midterm elections at home. Ukraine briefly acceded to the request, but has since resumed attacks – and Russia has continued to pound Ukraine’s energy infrastructure throughout the week. The latest reprieve by Trump for Moscow’s depleted coffers quickly triggered criticism from both sides of the aisle in Washington on Friday evening. The forestalled legislation would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% on – among other things – goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, the sale of which is crucial to funding the Kremlin’s war machine. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States,” Trump said in the order released by the White House on Friday. The order did not specify why the decision served the national interest, and said the waiver will remain in effect until the Trump administration determines that “further action is appropriate.” The measures were included in the Graham Act, legislation named after former Senator Lindsey Graham, a noted Russia hawk who died in July. Kirill Dmitriev, head of Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, hailed the waiver in a post on X as “an important and truly historic moment,” adding that “economic cooperation between Russia and the United States serves the interest of both nations.” US legislators, however, condemned the waiver. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren called it an “abject and predictable failure in leadership,” citing “strong bipartisan support” for Ukraine. Republican Rep. Don Bacon said Trump “is prolonging the war, not ending it.” In a post on X, Don Beyer, who represents Virginia in the House, said: “Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression.” And Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who helped draft the bill, said on X: “These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin.” A bitter feud The turnaround caps a turbulent week for US-Ukraine relations that has fueled concerns in Washington and Europe that Trump is taking a series of steps to actively help Putin. Trump blindsided European leaders last week when he struck a deal allowing Russian diesel exports – a move Zelensky said had left him feeling betrayed. The deal also drew bipartisan blowback at home. The US president has blamed the rise in fuel prices on the Ukraine-Russia war, eager to deflect attention from his war in Iran which remains deeply unpopular with voters. Ties between Ukraine and its most important backer the United States have also been strained by the apparent withdrawal of US intelligence sharing, and restrictions to the Starlink satellite internet service. Earlier this week, Zelensky said his government had received “no early warning from our partners” before a deadly ballistic missile attack hit a major power plant in Kyiv and damaged a residential building. Trump, however, said the US had not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. And Ukrainian authorities have said they were caught off-guard by restrictions on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink, disrupting operations of Ukraine’s drone missions and early-warning systems, and reducing the military’s capabilities for frontline logistics, communications and reconnaissance. Zelensky said on Friday that the Starlink operations had improved but had not yet been fully restored. Trump also lashed out at the Ukrainian leader in an interview with Newsmax on Thursday, saying: “I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.” Rising tensions come as CNN reported that Kyiv has run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, even as Russia continues to launch devastating air and drone strikes against Ukrainian energy plants. The interceptors are among the few defensive weapons capable of knocking down a ballistic missile, and Zelensky has been vocal about his constant struggle to obtain more stocks. Meanwhile, European leaders are rallying around Zelensky. In a veiled swipe at Trump on Friday, the Ukrainian president praised “real leaders” in the continent at a summit in Belgium. European Union leaders said they were preparing a new package of sanctions against Russia – the 22nd package since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In contrast with the Trump administration, they were keen to stress that sanctions against Moscow would be strengthened unless Putin stops the war.

articles.body: A teacher and an armed father stopped the teenage gunman who opened fire at an Oregon elementary school, killing three children and a teacher, as police investigate the motive behind the attack.According to Reuters, Police chief Mike Krantz said the teacher threw her cellphone at the gunman before tackling him and attempting to disarm him.An armed father, Kaylub Giamanco, 36, then entered the classroom and shot the teenager, killing him before police arrived. articles.title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
articles.summary: The US president temporarily ends many restrictions on Moscow recently passed by Congress over "national security" concerns.
articles.body:
Donald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.

The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by Trump in September.

But the US president issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US "national interest", prompting a backlash from US lawmakers.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed this week, after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel. Ukraine then accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.

Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another throughout the week. Ukraine's president barbed that it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said he was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy, giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.

It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.

Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump.

Democrats such as the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer have already criticised Trump's sanctions move, accusing him of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky.

"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X.

The move is also likely to draw criticism from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for tighter international sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort.

Trump initially drew criticism from Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel as a latest effort to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.

Trump has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Middle East conflict - which has sent fuel costs, in particular diesel, soaring - ahead of the US midterm elections. Rising inflation has soured Trump's standing with the American public.

Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.

A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel.

Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow says it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military.

Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days, and several fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.

This prompted scathing criticism from Trump, who said the strikes were a "disgrace". Zelensky replied that he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests".

There was fresh acrimony when Zelensky accused the US of deliberately slowing down an internet uplink via Starlink satellites used extensively by the Ukrainian military for defensive operations, as well as withdrawing intelligence-sharing.

During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning.

Zelensky said on Friday that Starlink speeds had still not been fully restored.

Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing and deliberately slowing down Ukraine's Starlink network.

articles.title: China invites Katie Zacharia to visit again after she claims nation lacks ‘proper toilets’
articles.summary: Beijing has invited now-ousted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia to visit China more often after she claimed the country lacks “proper toilets” in a recent interview.
articles.body: Beijing has invited now-ousted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia to visit China more often after she claimed the country lacks “proper toilets” in a recent interview. Zacharia, who was sacked by President Donald Trump less than a week into her job following an onslaught of scrutiny, came under fire for her lavatory remarks while speaking with far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec on Thursday. “I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking, how is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets,” she said, while discussing a perception around the lead-up to the US election in 2016 that the golden days of America were over, and that China was on the rise. When asked about those remarks on Friday, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning quipped: “She’s welcome to come and see China more often when she has the opportunity.” On China’s popular X-like social media Weibo, many called Zacharia’s comments “foolish,” while others admitted some toilets a decade ago were lacking in standards. Since reforming and opening up its economy in the late 1970s, China has barreled its way to becoming the world’s second-largest economy, with hundreds of millions lifted out of poverty and a nation transformed. But development inequality remains acute, especially between cities and more rural or remote areas. Zacharia’s time in China was just one of her career highlights that triggered intense media scrutiny following her brief and turbulent appointment as White House press secretary. A White House official previously told CNN that Zacharia had lived in China with her husband. On her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia lists herself as having worked as an “associate” in the international practice team at one of the largest law firms in the country, Zhong Lun, in Beijing for nearly two years starting in 2011. Zacharia had said in a statement she had “practiced international transactional law, with all the appropriate credentials.” Only citizens can be licensed to practice law in China, according to the Ministry of Justice, so it’s not clear what kind of credential she might have obtained.

articles.title: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico
articles.summary: Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend Carter Rhoad were killed on a surfing trip in an apparent botched robbery.
articles.body:
A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each.

The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial.

The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.

The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".

The convicted killers' full names were not given for legal reasons, meaning they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.

The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.

At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.

Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.

The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

articles.title: Cameroonians await government reshuffle after Biya’s return
articles.summary: After 10 weeks abroad, Biya returned to Cameroon but has yet to appoint a new government or vice president.
articles.body:
Yaounde, Cameroon – Every weekday at 5pm, Elvis Mbi tunes in to the state broadcaster’s flagship radio bulletin, hoping to hear an announcement from President Paul Biya that could signal a change in Cameroon’s political leadership.

Biya, 93, returned to Cameroon on August 20 after spending about 10 weeks abroad. His prolonged absence fuelled speculation about his health and whereabouts, including unverified claims that he had died.

His return raised expectations of a government reshuffle, but no new government had been appointed by October 6. The vice presidency, restored through a constitutional amendment in April, also remained vacant.

“Every Cameroonian was expecting that upon his return home, he was going to change government, but nothing up to this moment,” 39-year-old Mbi told Al Jazeera.

In his December 31, 2025, address to the nation, Biya promised that a new government would be formed “in the coming days”. More than nine months later, the promised change had yet to materialise.

The vacant vice presidency has drawn particular attention since politicians approved a constitutional amendment in April restoring the position abolished in 1972.

Under Law No. 2026/002, promulgated on April 14, the president may appoint and dismiss a vice president.

The amendment provides for the vice president to assume the presidency on an interim basis if the office becomes vacant because of the president’s death, resignation or permanent incapacity.

The vice president serves the remainder of the seven-year presidential term under the conditions set out in the Constitution.

The reform establishes a formal succession mechanism while leaving the appointment of the vice president to Biya. The amendment does not set a deadline for filling the post.

“We all know the president needs assistance in order to execute state duties and that’s why we are anxiously waiting for the appointment, but nothing has happened yet to our greatest dismay,” Mbi said.

A disputed presidential decree purporting to appoint a vice president has added to the speculation.

In June, an individual delivered a sealed envelope to Cameroon Radio Television (CRTV) in Yaounde containing a purported presidential decree appointing a vice president.

The document appeared to bear the official seals of the presidency and a signature attributed to Biya, according to a government statement published by state newspaper Cameroon Tribune on July 1.

CRTV did not broadcast what the document said. The government said the decree had not been issued through the proper official process and confirmed that the individual had been detained and an investigation was under way.

For Jude Mutah, a Washington-based governance and democracy expert and director of member relations at the Corporate Council on Africa, the attention paid to the state broadcaster’s evening bulletin reflects public expectations of political change.

In the absence of clear information, rumours can gain traction, he said.

Cabral Libii, leader of the Cameroon Party for National Reconciliation and an opposition figure in the 2025 presidential election, has argued that appointing a vice president would matter beyond filling a vacant post.

“The vice presidency is not just another administrative post to be filled. Appointing your vice president means securing your leadership,” Libii said in a public appeal.

“A vice president of this calibre could help to mitigate the succession struggles that are currently paralysing collective action,” he added.

The leadership questions are unfolding as Cameroon faces other challenges, including a separatist conflict in its English-speaking regions and an armed rebellion linked to Boko Haram around the Lake Chad Basin.

Jason Healy, a sub-Saharan Africa country risk analyst at BMI, part of Fitch Solutions, said uncertainty over political leadership could weigh on investor confidence.

Healy warned that prolonged uncertainty could discourage some investors from committing to large, long-term projects. He also suggested that delaying appointments could be a political calculation by Biya, allowing him to retain control over the timing and composition of any changes.

Mbi Aziseh Azimboh, executive director of the Policy Lab for Civic Innovation and Community Solutions (POLITICOS), said prolonged uncertainty could slow government decision-making and delay reforms and public policies.

Government defends president’s prerogative

The government has defended Biya’s authority to decide when to make appointments.

In an interview with RFI in August, Communication Minister and government spokesperson Rene Emmanuel Sadi said the president had the authority to form a new government and determine when to do so.

“It is surely quite normal for him to take his time when entrusting such a high office to one of his fellow citizens,” Sadi said.

Elvis Ngolle Ngolle, a former minister and coordinator of the ruling Cameroon People’s Democratic Movement’s academy, said citizens’ concerns were legitimate but maintained that the president had the constitutional prerogative to act when he chose.

The presidency did not respond to an Al Jazeera request for comment.

For Mbi, his radio-listening ritual continues.

“No one knows anything any more. It is so disheartening when I tune in each time but don’t get the big news,” he told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Houthis close in on key Yemen city of Taiz: Why a global trade route is at risk
articles.summary: Yemen’s Houthi rebels are tightening their grip on Taiz, cutting key supply routes to the southern port city of Aden.
articles.body: Yemen’s Houthi rebels are tightening their grip on Taiz, cutting key supply routes to the southern port city of Aden. The advance threatens to deepen the government’s military crisis and could have wider implications for security around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints.According to Reuters, the Iran-backed Houthis have made gains around Taiz, the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in Yemen’s southern highlands. Government troops backed by a Saudi-led coalition are struggling to reclaim lost territory and reopen the road to Aden.Taiz has long been a government stronghold surrounded by Houthi-controlled territory. In recent weeks, the Houthis seized sections of the 200-km road to Aden, including around al-Turbah and al-Misrakh, encircling the city since early October.Government forces, backed by Saudi-led coalition airstrikes, are attempting to reopen the route but were still losing ground in mid-October.The fighting has also raised fears of a prolonged siege, with food, fuel and medical supplies running short for hundreds of thousands of civilians. The battle’s significance extends beyond control of the city, threatening to further weaken the government’s position and complicate efforts to secure vital shipping routes linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.Why Taiz is strategically importantTaiz has remained a major centre of resistance to Houthi rule since Yemen’s civil war escalated in 2015.Taiz occupies a critical position in Yemen’s southern highlands, between Houthi-controlled territory in the north and government-held areas around Aden in the south. Its location along key road networks makes it an important corridor for military reinforcements, commercial supplies and humanitarian aid.The city is also close to the western coastal approaches to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The narrow passage is a vital route for international trade, including shipments travelling between Europe and Asia through the Suez Canal.A Houthi takeover of Taiz could further weaken the internationally recognised government’s position in southern Yemen and make it harder for its forces to move between strongholds.Houthis continue to attack Saudi ArabiaYemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels have vowed to continue attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities as the conflict with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government intensifies.According to Reuters on October 14, the Houthis claimed responsibility for strikes targeting Saudi Aramco facilities in Dhahran, Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and an Aramco refinery. Saudi authorities reported a limited fire at the Aramco headquarters complex, while the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired towards Riyadh.The escalation follows a series of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including a deadly strike on Riyadh airport on October 10 that killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree warned that attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities would continue.On the Yemeni battlefield, government forces have launched a counteroffensive to recover coastal territory seized by the Houthis near the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait.The fighting has also deepened the humanitarian crisis, with food and medical supplies running low and more than 121,000 people displaced across Taiz province.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Broad, troubling trend': US lawmakers urge FBI probe into mass shooting plot at Illinois Hindu temple
articles.summary: The US Congressional Caucus on India has urged the FBI and the Department of Justice to investigate the alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting at a
articles.body: The US Congressional Caucus on India has urged the FBI and the Department of Justice to investigate the alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Illinois as a federal hate crime. IIn a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel on Friday, the caucus called for a thorough probe to determine whether anyone encouraged, assisted or coordinated with the 19-year-old suspect, either online or offline.“This plot did not emerge in isolation but reflects broader, troubling trends,” Congressmen Rich McCormick and Ro Khanna, co-chairs of the House India Caucus, said in the letter.The letter cited FBI data showing an increase in reported hate crimes targeting Sikh, Hindu and Buddhist communities in 2025. The lawmakers urged the FBI and the Department of Justice to investigate the alleged plot as a potential federal hate crime and bring all charges supported by the evidence.They also called on the agencies to “share timely threat information with state and local law enforcement and with Hindu temples, Sikh gurdwaras, and other South Asian houses of worship, and offer them protective resources”.The lawmakers further asked Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel to brief the caucus on threats facing Hindu and Indian Americans and the steps being taken by their agencies to address them.“Brief the Caucus on threats facing Hindu Americans and Indian Americans and the steps the Department and FBI are taking to address them,” they said.US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi earlier said he and his family were worshipping at the Hindu temple in Aurora when the alleged attack was attempted. “My family and I were worshipping at our Hindu temple in Aurora on Sunday when a white supremacist attempted a mass shooting targeting Indian Americans. I'm grateful to those who helped prevent a tragedy, but we must come together to confront the hatred that put so many innocent lives at risk,” he said.The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) on Friday also expressed deep concern over the incident. Addressing a media briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, “This is obviously a matter of deep concern for us. At the same time, it is something that shows or highlights the increasing cases of hate crimes and racial discrimination against the Indian communities in the United States.”Jaiswal said India had taken note of the action taken by US law enforcement authorities following the incident, but called on Washington to ensure the safety and security of Indian nationals in the country.The accused was arrested on October 11 after a colleague alerted authorities to suspicious electronic communications, according to investigators and local police departments.Investigators later recovered a document outlining the alleged attack plan, along with firearms, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition, tactical equipment, body armour and a manifesto titled “Why I Fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter's Manifesto)”, which expressed white supremacist views.Prosecutors alleged that the accused openly identified as a white supremacist and expressed an eagerness to kill Indian people. The allegations remain subject to judicial proceedings and have not been proven in court.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Expansion of Heathrow Airport would drive growth, chancellor Healey says
articles.summary: It comes after the prime minister refused to say whether he backed expansion.
articles.body:
Chancellor John Healey has said building a third runway at Heathrow Airport has "always been a case for growth" after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say if he backed the expansion.

Healey said airport expansion, including at Heathrow, had been "a big part of jobs and growth" in recent decades, speaking at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok.

His comments came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham was more sceptical, telling the BBC last month it was "a matter for London and Londoners".

Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves had put the airport's expansion at the centrepiece of an argument that Britain was open for business.

Earlier this week Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye warned that not building a third runway at the UK's busiest airport would be a "huge missed opportunity".

Healey told reporters: "The case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth."

He added: "The formal position now is that the consultation is closed, led by the Transport Department.

"We're reviewing those, and then further decisions and announcements will follow."

The third runway been debated for decades, with the project facing opposition from residents, politicians and climate campaigners.

Last year, Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying "a third runway is badly needed", and the government could not "duck the decision any longer".

Asked about the project in September, Burnham suggested it was an argument for London to decide.

"I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he added.

The Department for Transport has said it is "considering the appropriate next steps" following the public consultation on its National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow.

The airport's consortium of owners has said they need explicit backing from Burnham before the end of the year in order to proceed with the project.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier this week, Woldbye said it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project.

He said he hoped the prime minister would "come along" with the project, adding that a third runway was "not just for Londoners".

"Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK," Woldbye said.

Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.

The project, which has an estimated price tag of £33bn, would see hundreds of homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues .
