articles.title: Imran Khan next for Nawaz, Benazir-style exile deal? Pakistan opposition leader’s big claim
articles.summary: Pakistan opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai has claimed that jailed former prime minister Imran Khan is being pressured into an agreement similar to
articles.body: Pakistan opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai has claimed that jailed former prime minister Imran Khan is being pressured into an agreement similar to arrangements that led former premiers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto into exile, according to a report by Dawnpublished on Saturday.Achakzai, chairman of the Pakhtunkhwa Milli Awami Party (PkMAP) and leader of the opposition in Pakistan's National Assembly, made the claim at a news conference at the Peshawar High Court on Friday. He alleged that the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) were involved in a similar political arrangement.“The same is happening today with the PML-N and PPP in government,” Achakzai said, according to Dawn.The claim comes amid political tensions surrounding Imran Khan, founder of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), who remains in prison, and opposition allegations over restrictions on political activity and the functioning of elected institutions.Achakzai was accompanied by Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) leaders Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas. He said opposition parties were in contact and that a multi-party conference would be convened soon. He also said resigning from the assemblies remained an option, adding that the opposition had submitted its demands in response to an offer of negotiations.What happened in Nawaz Sharif, Benazir Bhutto's exile cases?Achakzai's remarks referred to the circumstances in which Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, two of Pakistan's most prominent former prime ministers, spent periods outside the country following political upheavals, Dawnreported.Sharif was ousted and imprisoned after a military coup led by then-army chief Pervez Musharraf. He left Pakistan in 2000 under a deal negotiated with the involvement of Saudi and Lebanese leaders.Bhutto, meanwhile, went into self-imposed exile after her Pakistan Peoples Party lost the 1997 general elections, following her dismissal by then-president Farooq Leghari. Her husband, Asif Ali Zardari, was imprisoned on corruption charges and was released in 2004.Achakzai's comparison suggests that he believes a similar arrangement could be pursued in Khan's case. However, his remarks, as reported by Dawn, did not establish that an exile agreement involving the PTI founder had been reached.Achakzai demands access to prisoners, empowered parliamentDuring the news conference, Achakzai criticised restrictions on prisoners' access to meetings and called for changes to what he described as a "wrong amendment". He also demanded that parliament be empowered and an independent commission be established to ensure transparent elections.“Nowhere in the world is a prisoner denied meetings,” he said, according to Dawn.He argued that political disputes could not be resolved without strengthening parliament. He also expressed concern over the whereabouts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's chief minister and other lawmakers, demanding that the authorities disclose the chief minister's location.“We stand with the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The people of this province have the first right over its minerals. Regardless of political affiliation, everyone must unite for the homeland,” he said, adding that they would be safer if the country survived.Mengal, who accompanied Achakzai, criticised the government's actions in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and questioned the imposition of governor's rule on grounds of terrorism. He also alleged that elected representatives had been displaced and questioned the legitimacy of the political system.Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, also criticised the situation, saying: “You cannot run a country, yet you have occupied a province,” according to Dawn.Opposition challenges governor's rule in Khyber PakhtunkhwaSeparately, TTAP leaders approached the Peshawar High Court on Friday, challenging the proclamation of emergency and the imposition of governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.According to Dawn, the petitioners asked the court to declare the October 11 proclamation, issued under Articles 232(1) and 234 of Pakistan's Constitution, unconstitutional and without lawful authority. They argued that the constitutional conditions required for imposing the measures had not been met or that the government had exceeded its powers.The petition also challenged the purported transfer of the provincial assembly's legislative powers to parliament, the displacement of the elected chief minister and provincial cabinet, and the establishment of the proposed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Advisory Council and Area Development Secretariat.The petitioners sought the annulment of executive orders and notifications linked to the proclamation, including the deployment of armed forces to the extent that it allegedly violated constitutional requirements.They also requested interim relief to prevent the displacement of elected institutions and restrictions on elected representatives while the court considers the case.The legal challenge adds to the opposition's broader campaign against federal intervention in the province, as Achakzai seeks to bring opposition parties together over constitutional issues, political rights and negotiations with the government.You use AI every day. articles.title: The Israeli politicians seeking to replace Netanyahu
articles.summary: A look at Israel’s main opposition leaders, their parties and their largely shared positions on Gaza and other wars.
articles.body:
On September 26, five leading members of Israel’s self-styled Zionist opposition signed a non-aggression pact, seeking to oust incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in the October 27 election.

Gathered at the Tel Aviv home of opposition leader Yair Lapid were his co-runner, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of Beyachad; former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the new Yashar party; Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party; and Avigdor Liberman, head of the Yisrael Beiteinu party.

In the statement of principles published after the hours-long meeting, the leaders said, “Despite ideological differences among us, the formation of a Zionist, statesmanlike government dedicated to repair and reconstruction is our shared overarching goal.”

However, whether they offer meaningful change in substance as well as style, or which one of them might lead a future coalition, remains open to question .

With the exception of Golan, all take a fundamentally right-wing approach to Israel’s challenges.

None is committed to establishing a Palestinian state, with only the Democrats acknowledging it as a distant, unspecified goal. None, Golan included, accepts that Israel’s war on Gaza amounts to genocide or that it has committed war crimes in killing more than 74,000 people there. Nor has any questioned Israeli military actions against Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Qatar and Iran, instead reserving criticism mostly for how those actions have allowed Israel to be perceived internationally.

“The dominant forces in the opposition such as Bennett, Liberman or Eisenkot represent right-wing politics,” said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London. “They are not willing to touch the real, fundamental issue which is at the heart of everything: the Palestinian issue, and the Palestinian aspirations for independence.” He likened them to Netanyahu, but without the corruption allegations and support of far-right figures, such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. “Israel as a whole is a right-wing nation,” he added.

So, who are the main opposition figures and what do their parties stand for?

Credited with originating the Dahiyeh Doctrine in 2008, involving “ disproportionate force ” and large-scale destruction of civilian infrastructure against groups such as Hezbollah and Hamas, Eisenkot served as Israeli military chief from 2015 to 2019.

The 66-year-old entered politics in 2022 with former Defence Minister Benny Gantz’s National Unity alliance and later joined the war cabinet assembled by Netanyahu after the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023. In December that year, his son Gal, 25, and two nephews were killed while participating in the genocide in Gaza, losses commentators say have helped forge a connection with an electorate that has come to see itself as scarred by war.

In June 2024, he quit the war cabinet alongside Gantz , accusing Netanyahu of lacking a strategy to end the war. A year later, Eisenkot founded the centrist Yashar (Straight/Honest), advocating for professional government, military service for all – including ultra-Orthodox Jews – and a state commission of inquiry into the failings before October 7.

While notoriously ambiguous on many of Israel’s foreign policy positions, he has been critical of the government’s reliance upon the United States in achieving its war aims, while not questioning those aims themselves. In June, he characterised Washington’s mediated negotiations with Tehran to end the war against Iran that Washington had embarked upon with Israel as “a deal taking shape far from here and far from Israeli interests” and, the same month, railed against US restrictions on Israel’s freedom of action in Lebanon.

Eisenkot has ruled out including the United Arab List, or Ra’am party, in a post-election coalition. In a September 26 Channel 12 interview , he said no Arab party would accept his conditions, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state.

Beyachad (Together) is the joint list announced in April 2026 by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, who served for a combined 18 months in 2021-2022 between Netanyahu governments.

Bennett, a 54-year-old longtime supporter of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, leads the list, with Lapid, the 62-year-old founder of the centrist Yesh Atid party, in second place.

Lapid has called his partner “a right-wing politician, but an honest one”. Neither has prioritised resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or supported a Palestinian state. Though their 2021 coalition included Ra’am, Bennett has acknowledged that this broke an electoral promise.

Lapid has been one of Israel’s most outspoken critics of how its genocide and multiple strikes upon its neighbours are perceived internationally, while rarely questioning the rationale behind those actions. Bennett, in contrast, is more outspoken in his hawkish views. A full-throated supporter of the country’s war on Iran, he also congratulated Israel’s military and security services for a September 2025 attack on Qatar’s capital, Doha, that targeted senior Hamas leaders as they met to consider a Gaza ceasefire proposal put forth by the US. A Qatari security official was killed in the attack, which drew condemnation from across the region and beyond.

They now seek a government composed solely of Zionist parties, also ruling out reliance on Arab parties.

The most hawkish voice at Lapid’s table, Lieberman, 68, founded Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) in 1999 to represent right-leaning Russian-speaking immigrants.

Once Netanyahu’s protege, Lieberman has ruled out serving under him or joining a coalition that includes the ultra-Orthodox or relies on Arab parties, which he calls anti-Zionist. He has also rejected a minority government, reportedly making him a principal obstacle to Eisenkot becoming the bloc’s prime ministerial candidate.

In November 2023, Lieberman repeated his 2018 assertion, made then as defence minister, that there were “no innocents in Gaza”. In February, he visited the Karem Abu Salem crossing, known as Kerem Shalom to Israelis, and accused Netanyahu’s government of funding Hamas by allowing the minimal humanitarian aid that has been permitted into Gaza.

The Yisrael Beiteinu leader has been a consistent supporter of Israel’s genocide and subsequent military actions. In September 2025, he joined other Israeli politicians in criticising Netanyahu for the apology to Doha that he had been forced to make by the Trump administration for that month’s strike, saying the apology was instead owed to the Israeli public. Equally, he has argued against any restraint in its invasion of Lebanon, telling the Jerusalem Post in March: “If once again we go for a limited operation, some manoeuvre near the border, maybe talk about a security zone, it’s complete madness.”

“Lieberman does not belong in this bloc,” said Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, an Israeli analyst with Atlas Global Strategies, arguing that his main motivation was hatred of Netanyahu.

However, Ben-Ephraim said, Lieberman “maintains a loyal base and is a crucial force in Israeli politics”. His core constituency is the former Soviet electorate, but he has gained wider trust through his perceived independence.

Observers say he could potentially return to Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc.

The only leader at Lapid’s table from the Zionist left and the only one open to working with Palestinian parties, Golan heads the Democrats, a liberal party that was formed in 2024 through the merger of Labor and the social democratic, secular Meretz.

A retired major-general and former deputy chief of staff, Golan, 64, earned domestic plaudits for driving south during the 2023 Hamas-led attack and helping repel it.

Golan is alone among many in the anti-Netanyahu bloc in his criticism of the government’s war aims, arguing that military achievements are being squandered without a coherent diplomatic and political strategy

In May 2025, two years into the genocide in Gaza, Golan sparked controversy when he told a news conference that a “ sane country does not kill babies as a hobby ”, accusing ministers of celebrating the starvation of Palestinian children in the territory. He later walked back the comments after widespread criticism in Israel. In October, while praising the achievements of the previous year’s 12-day war against Iran, he told party members that the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei at the beginning of the conflict was a “mistake”. “Not because he didn’t deserve to die,” he caveated, “only because it doesn’t serve the interests of the State of Israel.”

Despite his openness to working with Palestinian parties, in September, Golan backed the disqualification of Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Arab Balad party, over an article about October 7, drawing criticism from the Joint List – an alliance of the Arab-led Hadash, Ta’al and Balad parties – and commentators.

Roi Zur, a University of Essex specialist in Israeli politics, said that despite Golan and Lieberman’s ideological differences on security and conflict, there will be “no winning coalition without these two”. He added that concerns about a clash between them miss the point, noting that both oppose Netanyahu, favour secularisation and strongly oppose exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.

articles.title: Three Mexicans jailed for 158 years each for killing Australian, US surfers
articles.summary: A Mexican judge sentenced the three men for the 2024 murders a week after they were found guilty.
articles.body:
Three Mexican men have been sentenced to more than 158 years in prison each for the murder of two Australian brothers and their American friend during a surf trip on Mexico’s Baja California coast in 2024.

A Mexican judge in the coastal city of Ensenada, in Baja California state, ruled on Friday that Jesus Gerardo Garcia, alias “El Kekas”, Irineo Francisco “N” and Angel Jesus “N” would each serve 158 years and nine months in prison for homicide, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.

The defendants were found guilty a week ago of the murders of Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson, aged 33 and 30, respectively, and their American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, 30.

The case impacted Mexico’s tourism industry by exposing the risks foreigners face when visiting the country.

Previously, the Baja California State Attorney General’s Office requested the “exemplary sentence” of 210 years in prison for each defendant.

Antonio Otanez, president of the Baja California surfers’ association, welcomed the outcome, saying “justice has been served.”

Otanez acknowledged that the killings had caused a “major drop” in tourist visits, particularly by surfers, to the region known for its beautiful beaches.

The Robinson brothers and Rhoad travelled to Mexico in late April 2024 to surf at a beach in Punta San Jose, near the popular tourist city of Ensenada.

The three friends camped on the beach on the night of April 27, 2024. Authorities launched a multi-day search with help from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) after the men were missing for several days.

The bodies were found on May 3 in a well more than 15 metres (50 feet) deep, all with gunshot wounds to their heads.

Last week, the brothers’ father, Martin Robinson, said the “guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons, Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad, whose lives were so cruelly taken from them in 2024.”

articles.title: Russian attacks in Ukraine kill at least 8, cut power to 1 million
articles.summary: Russia strikes Kharkiv, Kramatorsk, Volyn and Rivne as Moscow presses its campaign against Ukraine’s power grid.
articles.body:
Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 60 across Ukraine, hit two shopping centres and cut power to more than a million people, Ukrainian officials have said.

The attacks on Friday struck nine regions. In the eastern city of Kharkiv, a 71-year-old woman and a 58-year-old man were killed and 12 people were wounded in strikes on three districts, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.

Two people were killed in Kramatorsk, a frontline city in the Donetsk region, and two more in the southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region.

In the northwestern Volyn region, which borders Poland, a drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight, Governor Roman Romaniuk said.

Drones also hit a customs terminal and set fire to about 10 trucks in the town of Kovel, on a major road from Kyiv to Poland .

In Rivne, drones hit a major shopping centre and other sites, killing one person and wounding seven, regional governor Oleksandr Koval said.

A shopping centre in Sumy, close to the front line, was also hit.

Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy said repair crews had restored power to more than a million people who lost it on Friday.

In Volyn, about 370,000 households lost power, with supply since restored to at least 100,000 of them.

The blackout could last at least 24 hours in the regional capital, Lutsk, Mayor Andriy Razumovskyi said.

Large parts of Rivne were also left without power.

Russia’s military chief told President Vladimir Putin on Friday that the military had allocated the assets needed to press its aerial campaign against Ukraine’s energy system.

Meanwhile, the United Nations said on Friday that civilian casualties in Ukraine had climbed steeply.

According to UN human rights monitors, at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded in Ukraine last month, 85 percent more than in September 2025.

Between January and September 2026, 2,570 civilians were killed and 15,211 wounded, almost 60 percent more than in the same period last year and more than twice the 2024 level, the report said.

“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, head of the UN’s human rights monitoring mission in Ukraine.

articles.title: Typewriter art honours literary legends at Colchester exhibition
articles.summary: Colchester Library will host 50 pieces of artwork made entirely with typewriters until 3 November.
articles.body:
An art exhibition of famous authors is being displayed in a library, with one twist - the pictures were all drawn entirely with a typewriter.

James Cook was a teenager and studying to be an architect when he stumbled across the niche hobby of creating art with a typewriter. Millions of social media views and some celebrity endorsements later, he has made his hobby a full-time job.

The 29-year-old from Braintree, Essex, said: "All of this happened by mistake. I was quite happy to do typewriter art as a hobby."

His latest exhibition took him three years to complete and pays homage to 50 esteemed authors; particularly fitting as many would have used a typewriter.

Interwoven into the text are a number of hidden messages and facts about the literary legends.

For example, the sentence "2,000 words every working day" is etched into Stephen King's portrait.

The American novelist is famous for setting himself this target and his work ethic led to more than 350 million book sales worldwide.

The free exhibition at Colchester Library is on until 3 November.

While Cook honours famed faces from before his time, he is well known among the stars of today.

In 2022, Hollywood actor Tom Hanks wrote a personalised note on artwork Cook had sent him.

The two-time Oscar-winner has been collecting hundreds of typewriters "for no particular reason" since 1978. Cook owns 100.

Another admirer was Yeardley Smith, the voice of Lisa Simpson, who reached out to him and received a personalised portrait for her trouble - with a special twist.

Cook used "the Holy Grail" of typewriters, which can type musical notes instead of letters, enabling him to add them coming out of Lisa Simpson's saxophone.

He said: "I'm very lucky and fortunate that I'm able to do something that I love."

In July, Cook was invited to Wimbledon to create a piece ahead of the men's final.

He said being on centre court under the spotlights at 03:00 BST was an amazing experience.

"You hear the sound of the typing ricocheting off all the seats around the stadium. "It was just so surreal," he said.

The piece took him six weeks as it involved animation frames, a "recent addition" to his work. The frames involve Cook typing 50 separate frames and then flicking between them like a digital flipbook.

Cook has not been tempted by AI, insisting that the time and effort it takes to complete his work is exactly the reason people enjoy it.

"I think people really appreciate the fact that it's all done by hand, the fact that a single drawing could take me a month to produce," he explained.

"If I'm lucky, in the space of a single year, I might be able to create 12 drawings."

Cook's next stop is New York City, as he has been commissioned to depict the famous Rockefeller Ice Rink for its 90th birthday.

It is a large attraction, so he is using a typewriter three times its usual size and the completed work will be made up of two million letters.

He has also been invited to depict the Statue of Liberty.

articles.body: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang has shared a lengthy post on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) thanking the researchers and engineers behind the company’s latest AI model launches, saying he is ‘so grateful for every one’ of them stressing that the team’s mission is far from complete. In a post following the launch of Meta’s Muse AI models, including Muse Wonder and the open-source Muse Spark, Wang described the releases as a major milestone for the organisation, which was formed a little over a year ago with the ambitious goal of building a frontier AI model withinPost by Alexandr Wang roughly a year. According to Wang, many observers believed the objective would be impossible, especially given the position of Meta's earlier Llama 4 models. However, he said researchers and engineers from both inside and outside Meta joined the effort and worked with urgency to achieve the target.Alexandr Wang talks about ‘audacious’ goalWang said MSL and its TBD team were set up a little more than a year ago with the aim of producing a frontier model within about a year. Given where Llama 4 landed, he called that goal “incredibly audacious.” “Many people told us it would be impossible,” he wrote. “We knew it was unlikely, but still worth doing.”He said researchers and engineers from inside and outside Meta joined the effort. “Every single person came in, picked up a shovel, and got to work with earnestness and urgency,” he wrote. “Nobody asked whose job it was.”‘No deadlines’Wang said the team deliberately set a principle of no deadlines when TBD started, even as it faced work across pretraining, post-training, reinforcement learning, multimodal systems, infrastructure, safety, data and frontier research. “There was no use setting arbitrary timelines,” he wrote. The aim, he said, was to get to work and build the foundations of a frontier research effort in record time. “Run after run, this team did exactly that.”‘A machine that builds new models’Wang said the lab has built a repeatable system for advancing at the frontier. “More than just the models we released this week, we have built a machine that builds new models,” he wrote. He acknowledged that it can sound like a cop-out to say labs can keep scaling by “turning the crank.” But, he said, “now I have seen it first-hand.” He added that he is proud of how quickly the team keeps improving the models.He described the team as “the most brilliant people I have ever had the opportunity to work with,” including people “who will chase a weird loss spike past midnight just because they need to know why.” Of the past year, he said: “I will remember this past year for the rest of my life.”Read Alexandr Wang’s complete post hereAfter an exciting week of launches (muse articles.title: Nightclubs are disappearing - and it's affecting young people
articles.summary: One young person said with no nightlife in their town they cannot "let loose and mess around".
articles.body:
Under-30s have described missing out on being able to "let loose and mess around" because of a "bleak" lack of nightlife where they live.

Henry Gannon said that growing up in Woking he had seen places for young people to gather and socialise "die away".

"Communal areas just seem to have vanished," he added.

Woking once had multiple late-night venues - now it does not have any traditional dedicated nightclubs left in the town centre.

Gannon blamed the situation on the cost of living crisis, which he said was "pricing out" those in their 20s from enjoying themselves.

"There isn't really anything to do for younger people who often don't have much expendable income," he said.

Alternative options, the 23-year-old added, were "Wetherspoons, sitting in the park or getting a prohibitively expensive taxi back from another town or city".

"I feel like I am missing out on a crucial part of being my age, which is being able to let loose, mess around and enjoy life.

A quarter of UK towns have lost all their nightclubs, the Night Time Industries Association (NTIA) said in 2025.

It added that one in six towns have no late-night venues left.

"These figures are a stark warning of the systematic erosion of Britain's nightlife infrastructure," said NTIA CEO Michael Kill.

"We are facing a national cultural crisis.

"The damage, as we see it, is increasingly irreversible. Once these venues disappear, they rarely return."

Adam said the nightlife situation in Tonbridge - where the last club closed several years ago - was "pretty minimal".

"There are some nice pubs and small bars, though most things close around midnight," he said.

But the 29-year-old, originally from the US, said he was drawn to Kent town as it was "quieter and more relaxed".

Still, Adam said, the lack of nightlife forced younger people to go elsewhere for a night out, which impacted the local economy.

"It is definitely a missed opportunity," he added.

While he recognised nightclubs were spaces for meeting others, Adam said there was also a trend of younger people going out and drinking less - which was good for their health.

The twenty-somethings going out - in the gym

The BBC previously heard from under-30s that were opting out of drinking culture and getting their "social fix" from the gym .

They said that alcohol-free socialising was empowering, avoided hangovers and let them meet like-minded people.

Others have also pointed to a cultural shift with more people skipping clubs for sober social events .

Finn Ashcroft, from Chichester in West Sussex, said after Covid "people were finding it harder to get out and socialise".

However, he said it was important to emphasise that many under-30s were "making do" without clubs and instead creating their own events.

While its traditional nightclubs had closed, Ashcroft said Chichester had plenty of spaces that could be used for music and dancing.

He told the BBC he had set up the event companies C-Side Sounds and Strictly Grooves to "push music locally" in these spaces.

"Students were champing at the bit for somewhere to go," he said.

"We've definitely helped nurture nightlife within the city."

The 22-year-old said the "most important thing" people looking for more nightlife where they live could do was "be vocal about it".

"They have the power to [get] local councils and governing bodies to make sure there are spaces for people... to make memories together."

articles.title: Charity recognises changes to needs in Jersey over 25 years
articles.summary: Help a Guernsey Child says it has provided in excess of £1.2m worth of essential support.
articles.body:
A charity that raises funds to provide children with "essential items" has said families are facing "changing pressures" as celebrates its 25th anniversary.

Help a Guernsey Child said since it was created in 2001 it has provided more than £1.2m worth of essential items, equipment, services and support to local children and young people.

The charity said in its early years it gave financial support to a number of larger community projects benefiting children but there was now an increasing focus on helping individual children and families.

Alex Jenner, from Help a Guernsey Child, said: "Over the past 25 years, we have seen significant changes in the types of support families require."

Jenner said despite changes in needs the charity's "purpose has remained the same, to ensure that children in the Bailiwick are not disadvantaged because they lack the essentials that every child deserves".

The charity said it works through professional referrers who know the children and families involved.

Applications for grants come in from social workers, health visitors, teachers, doctors, nurses and other frontline professionals and are considered individually by the charity's Directors.

The charity said the increasing focus on helping in individual cases meant providing something as "fundamental as a bed, flooring, white goods, clothing, safety equipment or a heating appliance, as well as specialist disability equipment and educational opportunities".

It added the nature of their work reflected the "changing pressures" faced by local families.

These included the rising cost of living and increased demand for essential household items and practical support, it said.

Jenner said: "A relatively small grant at exactly the right time can make a profound difference to a child's safety, wellbeing, education or independence."

articles.title: From fan art to Star Wars: How a film poster hobby became a Hollywood career
articles.summary: Paul Shipper creates artwork for some of the world's biggest film and TV franchises.
articles.body:
A film fan who began creating his own movie poster artwork for fun has gone on to work on some of Hollywood's biggest franchises, including Marvel, Indiana Jones and Star Wars.

Paul Shipper said he was spotted after sharing designs online, leading to opportunities that once felt like "a dream", inspired by the films of George Lucas and Steven Spielberg.

Among the projects he has worked on are posters and artwork for blockbuster titles including Avengers: Infinity War, Doctor Strange, Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, Star Wars: The Last Jedi, Obi-Wan Kenobi and Skeleton Crew.

The illustrator said becoming a movie poster artist had originally seemed a long way off, before the early days of the internet helped his work find an audience.

"It was just through kind of sheer dumb luck really and the internet that it happened," he said.

"Before you know it, there are people who see it who are connected with the movies and then all of a sudden you get asked if you're interested in working on a Steven Spielberg movie or something like that."

Shipper described himself as "a Spielberg and George Lucas kid", saying franchises such as Star Wars and Indiana Jones were the films that first inspired him to become an illustrator.

For Shipper, the appeal of poster art lies in being able to tell a story with a single image.

"You're trying to distill something within one image," he said.

"It is kind of like a trailer... there are posters that tell you too much, so there is a fine line."

Shipper, who primarily works with pencils, said every commission presents a different creative challenge.

Looking back over his career, however, he was struck by how consistent his artistic style had remained, despite working across a wide variety of projects.

He said he thought his work had earned recognition among collectors and film fans partly because it drew on the tradition of the illustrated movie posters that were once a familiar sight outside cinemas and in video rental shops.

Gareth Griffiths, founder of AMPjam Poster Convention, said Shipper was among a small number of artists still working in a style associated with some of cinema's most iconic promotional artwork.

"He is one of precious few people that the film studio could go to if they're looking for someone that creates in that classic 70s and 80s style," Griffiths said.

The pair are now involved in AMPjam Presents: We've Been Framed, a charity exhibition bringing together more than 60 artists from around the world.

Many are known for creating alternative movie posters, which offer fresh artistic interpretations of films rather than reproducing the original cinema artwork.

The show is currently running at The Jointworks in Birmingham's Jewellery Quarter and features original artworks inspired by films and television shows including Jurassic Park, Star Wars, Toy Story, The Lord of the Rings, Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory and Lilo & Stitch.

Their concept turns a traditional exhibition on its head, the pair said, with artists creating original pieces inspired by a film or television show and designing them to fit unusual vintage or repurposed frames.

More than 60 one-off works have been produced by movie poster artists from around the world.

Griffiths said the idea grew out of his love of collecting film posters and pop-culture artwork.

During the Covid pandemic he launched online poster conventions after many fan events were cancelled, helping to build an international community of artists and collectors.

While the exhibition's reach is international, its roots are firmly in the West Midlands.

Shipper is based in Stourport, Worcestershire, while Griffiths, who organised the event, is also from the county.

The exhibition remains on display throughout October, with visitors able to view the artworks free of charge. Although donations are encouraged in support of Edward's Trust, a bereavement charity supporting parents, children and young people across the West Midlands.

Once the four-week exhibition comes to an end, every piece will be auctioned online, with all profits going to the charity.

Griffiths said he hoped the event would appeal not only to collectors but also to aspiring illustrators and young creatives interested in art and design.

"It's a rare chance to see original work from more than 60 artists in one place, meet people working at the highest level of the industry and learn more about the creative process behind some of the world's most recognisable film artwork," he said.

articles.title: The Voice singer Ciiara Nyx says music helped her navigate her trans identity
articles.summary: The 21-year-old Worcestershire singer says she is now "very sure of who I am".
articles.body:
A singer who won over all four coaches on The Voice UK has said music helped her make sense of the "complex" feelings she experienced growing up as a transgender woman.

Ciiara Baker, 21, who performs as Ciiara Nyx, earned a coveted four-chair turn during the ITV talent show's blind auditions after performing Glory Box by Portishead.

Speaking to the BBC, she said songwriting had become an important outlet after she came out as trans at the age of 15.

"There was always this weird feeling, like I wasn't in the right body," she said on the programme. "I would steal all my mum's clothes. I would wear her makeup."

Ciiara said she did not fully understand those feelings at the time, but had more time to reflect during the Covid pandemic when "the world went quiet".

"I was scared of feeling it and dealing with it because it is a big thing and it's very complex actually for a young person to go through," she said.

She said music had given her a way to express emotions she found difficult to put into words.

"I've never really been good with maybe saying things, so putting it into music is a lot more of an easier outlet for me."

Originally from Worcestershire, Ciiara spent her childhood in Broadway, Malvern and Evesham before moving to London, where she is studying music at university.

Her audition impressed judges Kelly Rowland, Sir Tom Jones and McFly bandmates Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones, who share a double chair as one coaching team.

All four turned their chairs in a bid to mentor her, with Ciiara eventually choosing Fletcher and Jones.

Away from the stage, she credited her mother, Vicki, with helping her embrace both her identity and her ambition to pursue music.

Vicki said she had "always known" her child was transgender.

"I've had my tears," she said. "But I'd rather my girl here and be with me and that's the bottom line of it all, and she's happy."

She added that she had encouraged her daughter to be herself.

"I've always said to her, 'be the person you want to be', and she is doing that and I love that."

Ciiara will return to The Voice UK when the competition continues on ITV1 on Saturday from 20:35 BST.

articles.title: Shropshire stained glass artist's appeal for 'endangered craft'
articles.summary: Nathalie Hildegarde Liege hopes to raise £5,000 by 13 November to help preserve the craft.
articles.body:
An artist is hoping to inspire others to take up stained glass-making to help preserve the craft and its creations for future generations.

Nathalie Hildegarde Liege, a stained glass artist for about 30 years, has launched a crowdfunding appeal to create a library and study room at her studio in Wem, Shropshire.

She hopes to raise £5,000 by 13 November to create a "haven for future professionals and the wider public".

"We are listed as an endangered craft. There's no time to waste really," she said, adding the skills could "vanish".

Liege's Andrew Moor Library and Study Room project is named after the author of the first contemporary stained glass book she found 31 years ago.

She picked up a French translation of 'Contemporary Stained Glass' in Paris and said it "was the catalyst for my move to an exciting area for contemporary stained glass".

The crowdfunder has been boosted by £150 funding from the Mid-Counties Co-op community fund.

A future plan is linking with libraries so they can access the collection of about 150 books built up since her student days.

As a teenager, Liege said she found it difficult to find specialist books or afford them and now wants to help other budding artists.

"It took me a long time to first have just four or five books of the basics of the technique," she said.

The Heritage Craft Association put historic stain glass window-making on its endangered crafts "red list " in 2023.

It says crafts in this category, include those where there are "serious concerns" about the craft's ongoing viability, due to factors such as falling demand or the number of craftspeople.

Liege believes other people will enjoy the beauty of stained glass and creating it.

Growing up in a French dormitory town, she "barely experienced nature" and when she first came across stained glass, it was very memorable.

"It was a very vivid experience of light on that day and colours and story-telling," she said.

As she began learning about it, the artist believed other people would also gain similar experiences.

"It's an ongoing, living artwork really, which lives with the quality of the day, in terms of weather, mood, whatever, but mainly through the glass, the light and the textures of the glass and the way we paint on it," she said.

Liege's career begun with a Fine Arts degree in Paris and work at the prestigious Pompidou Centre.

She set up the studio for her business Couleurlive in Wem in 2024, and says the county is home to both beautiful historical and contemporary stained glass works.

She hopes her studio can become an inspiring place for others.

"I need to do something, what else could I do? Then I thought of the library corner," she said.

"I thought why not offer people appointments to come to my studio, have a room in which they could sit, look at the books, take an hour or two, three hours if they want."

She added people would need to book in advance as the studio was also a busy working space.

"Because it's in the work space I think it would also be very interesting for people to come in, because they would also see the glass, they would see the lead, they would see me doing things."

articles.title: AI fears are being weaponised
articles.summary: Tech giants are fighting to protect their monopolies from cheap open-source models. Fear is their weapon.
articles.body:
As the growth of artificial intelligence accelerates, it is already posing significant challenges to society. Companies have started laying off workers whose jobs AI models can now perform. The expansion of data centres has spiked energy consumption and increased the carbon footprint. AI agents are being used by malicious actors to automate the spread of disinformation. Algorithms are demonstrating bias, raising concerns about flawed application and discrimination by human-related technologies that use them. AI is being used to identify targets in warfare, leading to greater loss of human life.

These are complex problems that demand serious regulatory attention. Yet, today’s dominant AI policy conversations are rarely grounded in these immediate challenges.

Instead, the global discourse has been swept by apocalyptic prophecies. We see this doomsday narrative promoted by some within the AI industry and echoed at the highest levels of decision-making: from lawmakers like Senator Bernie Sanders championing bans on superintelligence, to cautionary messages from the Vatican, to former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton calling open-source AI a real threat.

It is entirely reasonable for global leaders to take these industry-amplified warnings seriously. However, this chorus of influential voices sounding the alarm about AI “existential risk” has inadvertently pulled our focus away from the multiple crises AI has caused, already affecting labour, the environment and communications.

Worse still, the public panic is being weaponised to enforce a modern regime of digital colonisation – the concentration of power in the hands of a few AI corporations in a handful of countries.

The doomsday narrative provides the perfect justification for regulations that would target open-source AI models, which are free or cheaper to use and allow users to modify them to fit their needs. The logic presented to lawmakers is simple and seductive: if advanced AI is a potential weapon of mass destruction, it can only be developed by a trusted few.

Under the banner of “safety”, tech giants are attempting to write the rules to protect their monopolies by shutting down competition from smaller, cheaper open-source AI models.

This directly mirrors historical colonial tactics: preventing local industry from developing to force total reliance on the “empire’s” exports.

Currently, the entire globe is dependent on these frontier AI systems developed by tech giants, especially the Global South, which lacks the resources to create its own AI models from scratch, now costing upwards of $100m in compute power alone.

The problem with using the dominant AI models is not only that they are costly, but also that they often fail in local contexts. Consider Kenya’s recent rollout of the AI-driven Social Health Authority (SHA) system. Because the imported model was built on assumptions that did not accurately capture the reality of Kenya’s vast informal economy, the system failed spectacularly, systematically overestimating incomes and overcharging the poorest citizens for healthcare premiums.

To be effective, frontier AI systems must be adapted to local data. Since building them from scratch is financially impossible for most, open-source AI serves as the only viable bridge for local innovators. More importantly, preserving open-source AI allows the Global South to step off the West’s treadmill of human-mimicking chatbots.

Developing nations do not necessarily need conversational AI systems; they need AI that can help tackle development challenges in areas such as energy, healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing and climate mitigation.

If we crush open-source AI out of a disproportionate fear of AI agents, developing nations lose the main mechanism they have to build their own sovereign tech ecosystems for development.

Furthermore, AI monopolies lock in users in a cycle of data extraction and severe cognitive dependency. We are already witnessing the early stages of cognitive degradation as users increasingly outsource their critical thinking, creativity, and agency to frontier AI systems.

This dependency creates a feedback loop where our growing reliance fuels more data extraction, which in turn builds even more capable systems that strip away human agency and centralise absolute control.

While the Global South is uniquely vulnerable due to historical inequities, this dependency traps anyone not at the frontier. Even wealthy nations in the Global North face the exact same threat of lock-in and extraction.

So what is the solution? Calls for AI bans are certainly not. Abandoning AI would mean letting go of a technology uniquely positioned to accelerate the discovery of new drugs and new solutions to the energy and climate crises. There is already evidence of this with the development of tools such as AlphaFold and MOFSeq .

Banning open-source AI models is also a bad choice. Safety does not negate equitable access to AI. We can, and must, fund robust safety research and implement rigorous testing for near-term breaches. But we cannot allow the fear of hypothetical futures to justify the deliberate consolidation of power in the present.

Safeguarding the future of AI means ensuring that its development is decentralised, transparent, and globally distributed. It means defending open-source innovation as a public good and a fundamental weapon against digital colonisation. It means proactively addressing the human cognitive toll of the technology, ensuring that AI serves to augment human intelligence rather than erode it. It means anchoring absolute accountability in humans, instead of anthropomorphising AI agents that possess no humanity.

articles.title: Ajay Devgn’s Mumbai bungalow faces BMC action over unauthorised construction
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The BMC has rejected the owners’ reply and deemed ongoing construction at actor Ajay Devgn’s Juhu bungalow unauthorised after they failed to
articles.body: MUMBAI: The BMC has rejected the owners’ reply and deemed ongoing construction at actor Ajay Devgn’s Juhu bungalow unauthorised after they failed to submit documents establishing that the work had civic approval.The bungalow, located at Kapol Cooperative Housing Society in Juhu, is owned by Devgn and his mother, Veena Devgn.In a speaking order dated October 6, the BMC’s K/West ward office said the reply submitted on September 15 did not include documents establishing that the construction was authorised or a copy of permission granted by the competent authority.On September 10, the civic body had issued a stop-work notice under Section 354A of the Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act, alleging unauthorised additions and alterations using Siporex blocks at CTS No. 841, Plot No. 10, Kapol CHS Ltd, on N S Road No. 11, JVPD, Vile Parle (West).The notice directed the owner or occupier to stop work immediately and submit the relevant permissions within 24 hours. It warned that the unauthorised structure and construction materials could be removed at the owner’s risk and cost if the directions were not followed. Police were also asked to monitor the site and remove those carrying out the work, if necessary.In its October 6 order, the BMC said permission from the competent authority was required for the ongoing construction. Since no supporting documents had been submitted, the owners’ reply could not be accepted and the work was deemed unauthorised.The order does not specify whether the civic body has since taken steps to remove the construction.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Ukraine and Europe have little choice but to work with Trump
articles.summary: Despite growing tensions over Russia, Kyiv and European leaders remain dependent on US support.
articles.body:
“It’s painful when President [Donald] Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday. The United States president’s much-discussed diesel deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, has become another source of tension between Washington and Ukraine and its European backers.

The reported disruption of Starlink/Starshield services on October 13-14, which wrongfooted Ukraine’s military, has added to those tensions. Service was later restored, and reports that the restrictions were imposed at the White House’s behest to pressure Kyiv remained unconfirmed.

Nevertheless, the two episodes have reinforced the impression of a widening rift between Ukraine and the US. On Friday, Zelensky accused Washington of continuing to throttle Starlink and promising the Russians new concessions.

Obviously, one needs to wait until the dust settles. Trump has tilted towards Moscow before, notably at his August 2025 summit with Putin in Anchorage, Alaska, only to return to conditional support for Ukraine amid Russian intransigence and diplomatic efforts by Kyiv and European leaders. The arrangement under which Europe pays for US weapons delivered to Ukraine is working, and the US continues to share intelligence with Kyiv despite reports that some critical information has been withheld.

The White House has also walked back proposals to recognise Crimea as de jure Russian, floated in its April 2025 peace framework, or to require Kyiv to withdraw from the entirety of its Donbas region. For their part, Ukraine and Europe have continued to go along with Trump’s diplomatic overtures to Moscow, led by his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

The diesel deal itself may yet unravel, given bipartisan opposition in Congress, including from Republican senators. Washington’s latest shift towards Moscow may, therefore, prove less significant than it currently appears.

The above is no reason for complacency on the part of Ukraine and its principal backers in Europe. They have plenty of reasons to worry beyond Trump’s unpredictability.

Chief among them is Putin’s resolve to ramp up the war. Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure are coming under daily attacks from ballistic missiles and upgraded jet-propelled drones while its air defences are struggling. The country is bracing for yet another tough winter. A propaganda war is unfolding in parallel, fuelled by the diesel deal.

Unlike Ukraine, Russia never embraced Trump’s proposal for a partial ceasefire on strikes against energy facilities. Yet Moscow is now portraying Kyiv as the spoiler after Ukrainian attacks resumed, including an attack on a refinery in the city of Ryazan on Thursday which Trump slammed as “a disgrace”.

Fighting has spilled over onto NATO’s eastern flank with ships transporting Ukrainian grain through the Black Sea attacked in Romanian waters. Russia is expanding its hybrid attacks in Europe to disrupt supplies of weapons and ammunition to Ukraine and sway public opinion in key countries such as Germany by sowing fear. In some corners of the European Union, there is a push to re-engage with Moscow. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico confirmed that the Slovak-Russian intergovernmental economic commission would resume work. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, praised Trump’s diesel diplomacy, even as Russian drones carried out strikes near Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast.

Paying for Ukraine is another headache for the Europeans. The 90-billion-euro ($101bn) loan the EU authorised in April might be exhausted well before the end of 2027. Some estimates suggest Kyiv would require an additional 70 billion euros ($79bn) for defence and civilian purposes in 2027.

That threatens to open a can of worms for EU member states, which are already negotiating the bloc’s 2028-2034 budget.

With some calling for deep cuts in spending, the controversial question of whether aid for Ukraine should come from Russian financial assets frozen in Europe is coming back with a vengeance. Trump is meanwhile calling for some of the money to be released.

The squabble comes before several major elections, notably the French presidential election in April and May as well as polls in Spain, Italy and Poland.

Given the fragility in Europe, it is remarkable that diplomatic and financial support for Ukraine has remained rather steady. “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” European Council President Antonio Costa said on Friday while appearing alongside Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels. “If we fall, 20 million Ukrainians will come to Europe,” Zelensky reminded everyone, “Stay strong, defend our country.”

In the run-up to the summit, the EU opened two clusters in accession talks with Ukraine and imposed a new round of sanctions on Russia. Zelenskyy came to Brussels after talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III in London on Wednesday.

But there is a limit to how much more the EU and the United Kingdom can do beyond what they are already delivering. They have already replaced the US as the principal international champions of Ukraine and de facto guarantors of its survival as a state. Becoming a member of the EU – or, at the very least, a closely integrated partner like Norway – is the best-case scenario for Kyiv in the long run.

At the same time, Europe lacks the political heft and the military capabilities to substitute for the US in the short term. That is abundantly clear on the battlefield. Although top European intelligence agencies can probably supply Ukrainians with some data, there is no EU alternative to Starlink. Europe cannot deliver enough air-defence systems and interceptors to fend off Russian attacks without US support. Faced with US unreliability, Europe is investing in these capabilities in pursuit of strategic autonomy, but even in the best-case scenario, these efforts will take a decade to bear fruit.

Most crucially, Europeans have little leverage they can use to bring Putin to the negotiating table. Sure, there might be positive incentives in the form of sanctions relief and the restoration of oil and gas flows. But any Russian response is likely to require pressure of some kind. The US has thus far failed to twist Putin’s arm – and under Trump has moved from sticks to carrots, dangling all kinds of “deals” mixing diplomacy and business. Part of the failure is due to the fear of escalation with another nuclear power; part of it is the current US administration’s opportunism. But the bottom line is that there is little reason to expect Europe can do a better job.

In light of all this, both Zelenskyy and the Europeans will probably fall back on the familiar approach: trying to keep Trump onside and smoothing over their differences as much as possible. They are probably hoping and praying that the current White House overture to Russia will fizzle out after the midterm elections. They will also tell Trump that the best way to secure his legacy is to stand firm against Moscow, a position that enjoys support among his fellow Republicans. The strategy is to wait it out: first the winter, then the Trump presidency.

articles.title: YouTuber Dhruv Rathee faces court warrants over 2018 video targeting BJP IT cell
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Delhi court has issued bailable warrants against YouTuber Dhruv Rathee in a 2018 defamation case, news agency PTI reported.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Delhi court has issued bailable warrants against YouTuber Dhruv Rathee in a 2018 defamation case, news agency PTI reported.The case stems from a video published by Rathee in May 2018, in which he allegedly claimed that the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) Information Technology cell had attempted to bribe a man to defame him. The video was posted on Rathee’s social media account and later retweeted by Arvind Kejriwal, who was then the Delhi chief minister.The complainant, Vikas Sankrityayan, also known as Vikas Pandey, subsequently initiated defamation proceedings against Rathee and Kejriwal over the video and its circulation.Earlier, on October 12, Judicial Magistrate Rahul Jain of the Saket court ordered fresh summons to Rathee after the complainant submitted that repeated attempts to serve him had remained unsuccessful since the proceedings began.The complainant’s counsel, advocate Samaksh Sharma, told the court that the summons had remained unserved for several years as Rathee primarily lived abroad. The court was informed, however, that Rathee was then in India and residing at an address in Gurugram, Haryana.The magistrate noted that Rathee had first been summoned on July 23, 2019, and that the complainant had continued to pursue service of the summons. The court allowed Pandey to accompany the process server and directed him to deposit the process fee within two days. The next hearing was scheduled for October 17, 2026.Separately, Rathee is facing a defamation suit before the Saket court over a video that allegedly claimed Lord Ram and Goddess Sita consumed meat and alcohol during their exile.The complainants, who identified themselves as Hindu devotees, alleged that the video hurt their religious sentiments. They have also sought an ex-parte ad-interim injunction restraining Google from restoring, hosting, uploading, sharing or disseminating the video, or any video with identical or similar content, after notice and verification of the URL, during the pendency of the suit.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Slick diplomacy: Trump’s crude u-turn on Russia sanctions bails out India
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: For months, MAGA supremo Donald Trump and his minions threatened to “crush” India’s economy for New Delhi’s purchase of
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: For months, MAGA supremo Donald Trump and his minions threatened to “crush” India’s economy for New Delhi’s purchase of Russian oil. The economics has now caught up with the rhetoric. Faced with soaring fuel prices at home and a widely forecast rout in the mid-term elections, the US President has reversed course and put most of the Russia sanctions on ice, effectively leaving India off the hook for now.The presidential U-turn, announced in an executive order issued on Friday evening (when governments typically drop bad/embarrassing news), invokes the president’s authority to waive provisions of the Graham Act passed last month “in the national interests of the United States.” Among them: 500% tariffs on Russian goods; 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas (which would include India); and 100% tariffs on the top facilitators of Russian sanctions evasion.The waiver follows Trump's surprise announcement of a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel fuel, even as his administration has turned on Ukraine to end a war that began with Russia's invasion. The deadline to implement the sanctions was to expire on Sunday, one month from the day the bill was passed.This does not mean sanctions threat has disappeared. The executive order leaves the administration room to reverse course if Trump or designated officials later decide that further action is appropriate. In theory, the president retains leverage; in practice though, a threat that is announced, legislated, signed and then shelved risks becoming less an instrument of coercion than a negotiating prop.For India, which faced the prospect of tariffs as high as 100 per cent on goods entering the American market under the legislation, the reprieve is welcome -- and well may it send a bill to Washington for economic advice rendered. New Delhi repeatedly insisted that its energy purchases are governed by market conditions, supply security and affordability -- the very argument now being made by Washington. It also maintained steadfastly that its energy decisions cannot simply be dictated by the political preferences of Western capitals.While the presidential order is admirably concise about the legal manoeuvre, it is considerably less forthcoming about the political embarrassment and diplomatic debacle -- arising mainly from the vituperative hectoring the bill’s authors subjected India to. “If you keep buying cheap Russian oil… we will tariff the hell out of you and we're going to crush your economy,” raged the late Senator Lindsay Graham, who piloted the legislation, warning of tariffs up to 500 per cent. India survived; Graham did not, passing away on July 11 at 71.Graham’s Democratic co-sponsor Richard Blumenthal was scarcely more restrained. “To China and India: You better clean up your act. Buy your oil and gas somewhere else. Appeasement is not a strategy,” he declared. On Friday, Blumenthal was left fuming at Trump’s appeasement, accusing him of standing “on the side of a bloodthirsty thug and the enablers of Russia’s war machine.”Forgotten amid the hand-wringing: The Biden administration tacitly encouraged--and explicitly permitted -- India to purchase Russian oil to stabilize global energy supply so long as those purchases adhered to the price cap mechanism. Now, with Graham gone but his legislation very much alive, Trump has discovered that appeasement may not be a strategy either -- but neither is making American motorists pay a premium for geopolitical virtue.For India, the reprieve is reason enough for a quiet celebration. It was not exactly a Taco Tuesday, but it was certainly a Samosa Saturday in New Delhi: the country Trump threatened to crush for buying cheap Russian oil has been let off the hook by a president who has now discovered the virtues of affordable energy. The oil hasn’t changed, nor has the argument. Only Washington’s position has.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
